A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-3}} by the transitive property of equality." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ In $\text{L3}$ we have $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t),$ and in $\text{L4}$ we have $Φ(t)c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).$ Since both expressions are equal to the same quantity, the transitive property of equality gives $x(t)=Φ(t)c.$ Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3 and L4}.$" :question/difficulty For example, the line $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{EF}$ in the diagram below is a transversal.

![](images/cd/cdae3e21ca7b66c756e047b2f71dd03d1320a947e7477f6b025dacef95321399.png)

A pair of parallel lines with a transversal form a set of $8$ angles, shown below.

![](images/a4/a4465bbe051f978925e704cc40ced894c4e8c6625c53c7bd944a93c123359ab9.png)

This set of eight angles can be grouped into two categories:

- We have four pairs of **vertical angles**:

![](images/e0/e010db0c586e29e8ae640842f1519da314455bb7520680b80530799509058df3.png)

- We also have four pairs of so-called **corresponding angles**:

![](images/d1/d1b3f1ede08e3c20c80b7a23477491237e73a9b6691d93e6deabc5e5a4e0c57b.png)

Corresponding pairs of angles are located in the same position as each other relative to the parallel lines and on the same side of the transversal. Pairs of corresponding angles are congruent." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186070008 :tutorial/content "Consider the following pair of parallel lines $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{AB} \parallel \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{CD},$ and the transversal $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{EF}.$

![](images/af/af403ef4827e840a49d5a3bde36561d22a508d262b3ad15b830812aefc306286.png)

 What is the value of $x?$

First, note that $\angle DIF$ and $\angle BJI$ are corresponding angles. Therefore, they are congruent and thus have the same measure. This means we can write down the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠DIF & =m∠BJI \\ 3x-{20}^{∘} & =x+{10}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this equation, we first subtract $x$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-{20}^{∘} & =x+{10}^{∘} \\ 3x-{20}^{∘}-x & =x+{10}^{∘}-x \\ 2x-{20}^{∘} & ={10}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we add $20^\circ$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-{20}^{∘} & ={10}^{∘} \\ 2x-{20}^{∘}+{20}^{∘} & ={10}^{∘}+{20}^{∘} \\ 2x & ={30}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides by $2{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & ={30}^{∘} \\ \frac{2x}{2} & =\frac{{30}^{∘}}{2} \\ \frac{\cancel{2}x}{\cancel{2}} & ={15}^{∘} \\ x & ={15}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=15^\circ.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068954 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162109 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-3039fef2-75f2-578d-b446-f0e62f788f69"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162110 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e261753e-ab38-5195-b690-27439e259444"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162111 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-c677bfcd-f9c7-587b-870f-9f5be736939b" "question-18e0dc2d-9409-5746-a133-14c7fa279d0a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-3039fef2-75f2-578d-b446-f0e62f788f69" :question/id #uuid "3039fef2-75f2-578d-b446-f0e62f788f69" :question/math-academy-id "q-143270" :question/problem "Given that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{25}∼N(-6,{15}^{2})$ is a random sample of size $n=25$ from a normal population, what is the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}?$" :question/worked-solution "If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| $\,0.3\,$ | $\,0.6179\,$ | $\,0.6217\,$ | $\,0.6255\,$ | $\,0.6293\,$ | $\,0.6331\,$ | $\,0.6368\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(7,\frac{{14}^{2}}{49}) \\  & ∼N(7,4).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7.5).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7.5) & =P(\frac{6.8-7}{\sqrt{4}}<Z<\frac{7.5-7}{\sqrt{4}}) \\  & =P(-0.1<Z<0.25) \\  & =Φ(0.25)-Φ(-0.1)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.25)=0.5987,\end{aligned}
$$

and by the symmetry of the normal distribution,

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.1) & =1-Φ(0.1) \\  & =1-0.5398 \\  & =0.4602.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7.5) & =Φ(0.25)-Φ(-0.1) \\  & =0.5987-0.4602 \\  & =0.1385.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a6304b95-a451-5219-83db-3e96f7493cf2"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

 then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

We're told that the population mean $\mu =20,$ the population standard deviation $\sigma =1,$ and that the sample size $n=50.$ Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(20,\frac{{1}^{2}}{50}) \\  & ∼N(20,0.02).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(19.9<\overset{―}{X}<20.1).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(19.9<\overset{―}{X}<20.1) & =P(\frac{19.9-20}{\sqrt{0.02}}<Z<\frac{20.1-20}{\sqrt{0.02}}) \\  & =P(-0.71<Z<0.71) \\  & =Φ(0.71)-Φ(-0.71)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.71) & =0.2389 \\ Φ(0.71) & =0.7611.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(19.9<\overset{―}{X}<20.1) & =Φ(0.71)-Φ(-0.71) \\  & ≈0.7611-0.2389 \\  & =0.5222.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-6aa7ff90-9f47-5592-8679-5038f72e40c3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-6aa7ff90-9f47-5592-8679-5038f72e40c3" :answer-field/id #uuid "6aa7ff90-9f47-5592-8679-5038f72e40c3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-f115bc70-f615-5164-bacc-05e1c087475f" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3953291d-ec18-59f1-bd5e-8ffdf3868a64" "answer-ce5f155f-12d7-53aa-abbf-116bd0ec73d2" "answer-efb2cb42-09d9-5f87-983c-37bafdc44ab0" "answer-f115bc70-f615-5164-bacc-05e1c087475f" "answer-0d2d79f1-f5df-56c1-a632-32e686a02c5e"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3953291d-ec18-59f1-bd5e-8ffdf3868a64" :answer/id #uuid "3953291d-ec18-59f1-bd5e-8ffdf3868a64" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.3900" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ce5f155f-12d7-53aa-abbf-116bd0ec73d2" :answer/id #uuid "ce5f155f-12d7-53aa-abbf-116bd0ec73d2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.4514" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-efb2cb42-09d9-5f87-983c-37bafdc44ab0" :answer/id #uuid "efb2cb42-09d9-5f87-983c-37bafdc44ab0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.4648" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f115bc70-f615-5164-bacc-05e1c087475f" :answer/id #uuid "f115bc70-f615-5164-bacc-05e1c087475f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.5222" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0d2d79f1-f5df-56c1-a632-32e686a02c5e" :answer/id #uuid "0d2d79f1-f5df-56c1-a632-32e686a02c5e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.5284" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162387 :question/problem "The weights of a particular breed of geese are normally distributed with a mean of $7\,\text{kg}$ and a standard deviation of $1\,\text{kg}.$ Suppose $4$ geese are randomly selected. We're told that the population mean $\mu =7,$ the population standard deviation $\sigma =1,$ and that the sample size $n=4.$ Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(7,\frac{{1}^{2}}{4}) \\  & ∼N(7,0.25).\end{aligned}

We're required to find $P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7).$

$$

From the table, we have

$$
Φ(-0.4)=0.3446.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7) & =0.5-Φ(-0.4) \\  & =0.5-0.3446 \\  & =0.1554.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186159524 :answer-field/correct 17592186159527 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-18e0dc2d-9409-5746-a133-14c7fa279d0a" :question/id #uuid "18e0dc2d-9409-5746-a133-14c7fa279d0a" :question/math-academy-id "q-143452" :question/problem "The weights of sugar in different types of cookies are normally distributed with a mean of $15\,\text{g}$ and a standard deviation of $2\,\text{g}.$ Suppose $16$ cookies are selected randomly. variation, $y=5$ when $x=8.$ Find an equation that relates $x$ and $y.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $y$ varies inversely with $x,$ we use the equation

$$
y=\dfrac{k}{x}.
$$

Next, we use the data $y=5$ when $x=8$ to find $k\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =\frac{k}{8} \\ 5\cdot 8 & =k \\ 40 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our inverse variation equation is

$$
y = \dfrac{40}{x}.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186138414 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-157c2ce3-5327-5267-a129-7f9aebf9b49f" "question-19618a93-f5c7-57b8-b5e4-4ba96b1ca9c7"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186138170 :question/problem "If $y$ varies inversely with $x$ and $y=15$ when $x=\dfrac{3}{5}$, find the value of $y$ when $x=3.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $y$ varies inversely with $x,$ we use the equation

$$
y=\frac{k}{x}.
$$

for some constant $k.$ Note that we can rewrite the above equation as follows.

$$
x\cdot y=k
$$

So, we will compute $x\cdot y=k$ for each row in the table. If we get the same value of $k$ for each row, then we can conclude that $y$ is inversely proportional to $x.$

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $x\cdot y=k$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $4$ | $3.5$ | $4\cdot 3.5=14$ |
| $7$ | $2$ | $7\cdot 2=14$ |
| $14$ | $1$ | $14\cdot 1=14$ |

The results are all the same: in each row, we have $k=14.$ Therefore, we conclude:

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Since $y$ varies inversely with $x,$ we use the equation

$$
y=\frac{k}{x}.
$$

In the graph, we notice a point with $x=8$ and $y=\frac{3}{2}.$ We substitute this data into the equation to find $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} & =\frac{k}{8} \\ \frac{3}{2}\cdot 8 & =k \\ 12 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse variation equation is given by

$$
y=\frac{12}{x}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8df595bc-00dd-5e1e-9875-a07a226991b3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-8df595bc-00dd-5e1e-9875-a07a226991b3" :answer-field/id #uuid "8df595bc-00dd-5e1e-9875-a07a226991b3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-3d46e461-53f4-5a4c-aa29-7447146a4f04" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3d46e461-53f4-5a4c-aa29-7447146a4f04"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3d46e461-53f4-5a4c-aa29-7447146a4f04" :answer/id #uuid "3d46e461-53f4-5a4c-aa29-7447146a4f04" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{12}{x}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186139718 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we're making a juice drink with a fixed amount of pure orange and the rest water. 

The more water that we add, the less that we'll be able to taste the orange. 

More precisely, the concentration of pure orange $y$ (in grams per liter) varies **inversely** with the volume $x$ (in liters) of water added. We can express this idea using an **inverse variation equation** as follows:

$$
y= \dfrac{k}{x}
$$

The constant $k$ is called the **constant of variation** or **constant of proportionality.**

Notice that:

- If $x$ is small (i.e., there is not much water), then $y$ is large (i.e., there is a high concentration of orange).

- If $x$ is large (i.e., there is lots of water), then $y$ is small (i.e., there is a low concentration of orange).

To find the constant of variation $k$, we need to plug in some data. 

For example, suppose we know that the concentration is $y = 200\, \textrm{g/L}$ when $x = 4\,\textrm L$ of water has been added. Plugging this into our relationship and solving for $k,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{k}{x} \\ 200 & =\frac{k}{4} \\ 200\cdot 4 & =k \\ 800 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the relationship between $y$ and $x$ is

$$
y = \dfrac {800} x.
$$

Finally, notice that we can rewrite the above relationship as

$$
xy = 800.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186139720 :tutorial/content "If  $y$ varies inversely with  $x,$ then we can also say that $y$ is **inversely proportional** to $x.$ We can express this mathematically as

$$
y \propto \dfrac{1}{x},
$$

where $\propto$ is the proportionality symbol.

The following statements are equivalent:

- $y = \dfrac{k}{x}$ for some constant $k$

- $y$ varies inversely with $x$

- $y$ is inversely proportional to $x$

- $y \propto \dfrac{1}{x}$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186138599 :activity/expected-seconds 720.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [[17592186228929 :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $90\cos(6t)\,\textrm{V},$ a resistor with resistance $30\,\Omega,$ and a capacitor with capacitance $\dfrac1{150}\,\textrm{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I = \dfrac{\textrm d q}{\textrm d t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R = 30\,\Omega.$ So,

$$
V_R = 30I = 30\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore,

$$
V_C = \dfrac{q}{\left(\dfrac1{150}\right)} = 150q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
90\cos(6t) = 30\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 150q,
$$

which gives

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 5q = 3\cos(6t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution $q_c,$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q_c}{\mathrm{d}t} + 5q_c = 0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
q_c(t) = Ae^{-5t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $6t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $6t,$ i.e.,

$$
q_p(t) = \alpha\cos(6t) + \beta\sin(6t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-6\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+6\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-6\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+6\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t))+5(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ (-6\alpha +5\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+(5\alpha +6\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-6\alpha +5\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)) \\ 5\alpha +6\beta =3\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha = \dfrac{15}{61}, \beta = \dfrac{18}{61}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
q_p(t) = \dfrac{15}{61}\cos(6t) + \dfrac{18}{61}\sin(6t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t) = q_c(t) + q_p(t) = Ae^{-5t} + \dfrac{15}{61}\cos(6t) + \dfrac{18}{61}\sin(6t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity $q_c(t) = Ae^{-5t}$ is the *transient charge*, since it goes to zero as $t \to \infty.$

- The function $q_p(t) = \dfrac{15}{61}\cos(6t) + \dfrac{18}{61}\sin(6t)$ is the *steady-state charge*. It governs the charge's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to\infty,$ we have

$$
q(t)\approx q_p(t) = \dfrac{15}{61}\cos(6t) + \dfrac{18}{61}\sin(6t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state charge, in coulombs, is given by

$$
\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{15}{61}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{18}{61}\right)^2} \approx 0.38,
$$

rounded to two decimal places."] ["question-f1b0e27c-532b-588c-9b00-39b1140a6bd7" :question/id #uuid "f1b0e27c-532b-588c-9b00-39b1140a6bd7"] ["question-f1b0e27c-532b-588c-9b00-39b1140a6bd7" :question/math-academy-id "q-337052"] ["question-f1b0e27c-532b-588c-9b00-39b1140a6bd7" :question/problem "![](images/d5/d5be79e0c9f09b5810459bfd8a1ce88f21e2e709dff9d20d7369681ddb61a81b.png)

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{0.003}=\frac{1000}{3}q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
18=60\,\frac{dq}{dt}+\frac{1000}{3}q,
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}+\frac{50}{9}q=\frac{3}{10}.

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+\frac{50}{9}{q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-50t/9},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha .
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${q}_{p}=\alpha $ and $\frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt}=(\alpha )^{′}=0$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0+\frac{50}{9}\alpha =\frac{3}{10}\,⟹\,\alpha =\frac{27}{500}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is ${q}_{p}(t)=\frac{27}{500}.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t)={q}_{c}(t)+{q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-50t/9}+\frac{27}{500}.
$$

$$

$$

- The quantity ${q}_{c}=-\frac{1}{250}{e}^{-50t/9}$ is the *transient charge*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

Consider the RC circuit shown above. Given that the charge $q(t)$ of the capacitor at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$
q(t)=A{e}^{-t}+\frac{P}{425}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{Q}{425}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)
$$

where $A,$ $P,$ and $Q$ are constants, find the value of $P+Q.$

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*"] ["question-82951619-49dc-5358-8bd0-2dda9a341d9b" :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor with resistance $200\,Ω,$ and a capacitor of capacitance $0.005\,\text{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I=\frac{\text{d}q}{\text{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=200\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=200I=200\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{0.005}=200q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)=200\,\frac{dq}{dt}+200q,
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}+q=\frac{1}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+{q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $4t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $4t,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+4\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+4\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))+(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) & =\frac{1}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ (-4\alpha +\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+(\alpha +4\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & =\frac{1}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4\alpha +\beta =\frac{1}{25}\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\ \alpha +4\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{4}{425},\beta =\frac{1}{425}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=-\frac{4}{425}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{1}{425}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t)={q}_{c}(t)+{q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-t}-\frac{4}{425}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{1}{425}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Therefore, we have $P=-4,Q=1,$ and

$$
P+Q=-4+1=-3.
$$"] ["question-82951619-49dc-5358-8bd0-2dda9a341d9b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-d53980ff-5f51-516b-b4df-e3f2a87df48f" :answer-field/id #uuid Recall that the last two rules are known as the **distributive properties.**"] [17592186173140 :tutorial/content "We know that the absolute value operation does nothing to a number if it is non-negative. For example:

$$

$$

We can summarize this fact as follows:

$$
|x| = x \quad \text{ if } \quad x \geq 0
$$

If a variable is known to be negative, then the absolute value changes it to positive. To turn a negative number into a positive number, we multiply by $-1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
|x|  = -x \quad\textrm{for}\quad x < 0.
$$

To convince ourselves that this is indeed true, let's verify it in the case when $x=-2.$ Substituting this value into the above, we get

meters."] ["question-9c4f0f4c-398e-580b-8ef0-276b7b031bf0" :question/worked-solution "The width of the plot is $x-1$ meters, and its area is $2{x}^{2}-2x$ square meters. Since the $\text{area}=\text{length}\times \text{width},$ we factor the expression for the area to find the length.

First, we find the $\text{GCF}$ of the two terms:

$$
\text{GCF}(2{x}^{2},-2x)=2x
$$

Then, we rewrite each term in the original expression as a product with the $\text{GCF}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-2x & = \\ (2x\cdot x)+(2x\cdot (-1))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we write the $\text{GCF}$ outside the parentheses and keep the remaining terms inside:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2x\cdot x)+(2x\cdot (-1)) & = \\ 2x(x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we conclude that the length of the plot must be $2x$ meters.

First, we find the factor pairs of the constant term $(-6).$ The constant term is negative, so that means one of the factors is negative, and the other is positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & \times (-6) \\ (-1) & \times 6 \\ 2 & \times (-3) \\ (-2) & \times 3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find which factor pair adds up to the coefficient of the linear term $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1+(-6) & =-5 & \times  \\ -1+6 & =5 & \times  \\ 2+(-3) & =-1 & \times  \\ -2+3 & =1 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

Using the factor pair identified above, write the linear term as $x=-2x+3x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+x-6 & ={x}^{2}-2x+3x-6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately, and then factor the expression completely:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-2x+3x-6 & = \\ ({x}^{2}-2x)+(3x-6) & = \\ x(x-2)+3(x-2) & = \\ (x-2)(x+3)\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we conclude that the width must be $x-2$ meters.

$$
30\cdot (1.1)^{4}=43.923≈44,
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

"![](images/39/39a83b1081d22919c9549c4ff1c6ad8006dc802cc23f9802d762e97883bea48c.png)

Consider a sample of size $n=32$ from a normal population with standard deviation $\sigma =18.$ Given that the mean of the sample is $\overset{―}{x}=-67,$ find a $90%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu $ of the distribution.

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(Z>1.645)=0.05,$ where $Z∼N(0,1),$ as shown in the diagram above.*"] ["question-1c22a90f-9b7c-5ddf-a251-f5b0ff5c7b6d" :question/worked-solution "We are told that the population is normally distributed. Therefore, the distribution of sample mean is also normal, and we have that

$$
\frac{\overset{―}{X}-\mu }{\sigma /\sqrt{n}}∼N(0,1),
$$

where 

- $\overset{―}{X}$ is the sample mean,

- $\mu $ is the population mean,

- ${\sigma }^{2}$ is the population variance, and

- $n$ is the sample size.

Given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu $ of the original distribution is given by

$$
\overset{―}{x}\pm {z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}},
$$

where $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

We are interested in finding a $90%$ confidence interval. So, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.9=0.1\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.05.
$$

We are given that $P(Z>1.645)=0.05.$ As a result, 

$$
{z}_{\alpha /2}={z}_{0.05}=1.645.
$$

Therefore, a $90%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu $ is the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-67\pm 1.645\cdot \frac{18}{\sqrt{32}} \\ -67\pm 5.234\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-1c22a90f-9b7c-5ddf-a251-f5b0ff5c7b6d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-54346f0e-b0c5-52e5-ab1c-ea523499e32b" :answer-field/id #uuid *Hint: Use the fact that $P(Z>2.576)=0.005,$ where $Z∼N(0,1),$ as shown in the diagram above.*"] ["question-87f55a60-f84e-5cb1-9665-2c11dc9713b6" :question/worked-solution "We do not know the distribution of the population. However, the sample size $n=144\ge 30$ is *sufficiently large*. Therefore, according to the central limit theorem, we may use the following approximation:

$$
\frac{\overset{―}{X}-\mu }{\sigma /\sqrt{n}}∼N(0,1),
$$

where 

- $\overset{―}{X}$ is the sample mean,

- $\mu $ is the population mean,

- ${\sigma }^{2}$ is the population variance, and

- $n$ is the sample size.

Given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu $ of the original distribution is given by

$$
\overset{―}{x}\pm {z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}},
$$

where $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

We are interested in finding a $99%$ confidence interval. So, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.99=0.01\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.005.
$$

We are given that $P(Z>2.576)=0.005.$ As a result, 

$$
{z}_{\alpha /2}={z}_{0.005}=2.576.
$$

Therefore, the $99%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu $ is the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}10\pm 2.576\cdot \frac{2}{\sqrt{144}} \\ 10\pm 0.429\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-87f55a60-f84e-5cb1-9665-2c11dc9713b6" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-4fab1b25-a070-5368-a780-857e62a9b5a5" :answer-field/id #uuid distributed with standard deviation $\sigma =1\,200$ dollars. During a particular $28$-working-day month, the mean daily income was $1\,950$ dollars. Find a $90%$ confidence interval for the mean daily income $\mu $ of every work day.

*Hint: Given a random variable $Z∼N(0,1),$ the table below shows the $z$-scores ${z}_{p}$ such that $P(Z>{z}_{p})=p$ for some particular values of $p.$*

| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${z}_{p}$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $1.960$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |"] ["question-66172e40-7344-58fd-a3d5-83fcbd16bd0f" :question/worked-solution "We are told that the population is normally distributed. Therefore, the distribution of sample mean is also normal, and we have that

$$
\frac{\overset{―}{X}-\mu }{\sigma /\sqrt{n}}∼N(0,1),
$$

where 

- $\overset{―}{X}$ is the sample mean,

- $\mu $ is the population mean,

- ${\sigma }^{2}$ is the population variance, and

- $n$ is the sample size.

Given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu $ of the original distribution is given by

$$
\overset{―}{x}\pm {z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}},
$$

where $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

In our case,

$$
\overset{―}{x}=1\,950,\,n=28,\,\sigma =1\,200
$$

We are interested in finding a $90%$ confidence interval. So, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.9=0.1\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.05.
$$

We also need to find the $z$-score value ${z}_{0.05}$ such that $P(Z>{z}_{0.05})=0.05,$ where $Z∼N(0,1).$

![](images/2f/2fc6327df99c6b88508b0c4de2e4edf6c5521974f05e2e2f02d09786937285a7.png)

From the percentage points table of the normal distribution, we obtain that ${z}_{0.05}=1.645:$ 

| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.05$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${z}_{p}$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $1.960$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |

Therefore, the $90%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu $ is the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}1\,950\pm 1.645\cdot \frac{1\,200}{\sqrt{28}} \\ 1\,950\pm 373\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-66172e40-7344-58fd-a3d5-83fcbd16bd0f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-32c160c3-a273-5a41-b70a-aa88ce3a1e92" :answer-field/id #uuid random sample of size $n=10$ from a normal population with the unknown population mean $\mu$ and *known* population variance $\sigma^2=9.$ After processing our results, we compute the mean of this sample using the usual methods and get the following result:

$$
\overline{x}=12
$$

 

This is an unbiased estimate of the population mean $\mu.$ However, it is unsatisfactory because we have no information regarding its reliability.

For this reason, it's often more helpful to give a range of possible values for $\mu.$ In other words, instead of reporting a single estimate $\overline{x},$ we might instead report a so-called **confidence interval,** which is an interval of the form

$$
(\overline{x}-E, \: \overline{x}+E)
$$

 

where 

- $\overline{x}$ is our estimate of the population mean, and

- $E$ is some **margin of error**.

In addition, we need to give some indication regarding the reliability of our confidence interval. With this in mind, we will construct a $\boldsymbol{95\%}$ **confidence interval** for the population mean $\mu$. The precise meaning of this will become clear shortly."] [17592186060968 :tutorial/content "In our example, the population is normally distributed. Therefore, the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is also normally distributed, where

$$
\overline{X}\sim N\left(\mu,\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

By transforming $\overline{X}$ to a standard normal random variable, we have

$$
Z = \dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\sim N(0,1).
$$

We wish to find a $z$-interval that we're $95\%$ confident that the random variable $Z$ lies within. This interval is indicated in the diagram below:

![](images/50/50a0f49fe5c96ba3259832fbf1a0abcedffb342301ca069bb7b88d157a181019.png)

  

To help with the notation, we define a new parameter $\alpha.$ Since we're computing a $95\%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha=1-0.95=0.05\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.025.
$$

Notice that $\dfrac{\alpha}{2}$ is precisely the area bounded by each "tail" that we're excluding from our confidence interval. Let's label the critical values at the endpoints of our interval as $\pm z_{\alpha/2}\mathbin{:}$

![](images/3c/3cdfd2c72bf7fe65e5d1b584d46d4c846e74615e54c739a6d1ea990c95011a8a.png)

  

According to our diagram,

$$
P(Z > z_{0.025}) = P(Z < -z_{0.025}) = 0.025.
$$

  

Using a percentage points table for the standard normal distribution, we find that $z_{0.025} \approx 1.96.$ Therefore,

$$
P(Z > 1.96) = P(Z < -1.96) = 0.025.
$$

In other words,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.96<Z<1.96)=0.95.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, there is a $95\%$ probability that our random variable $Z$ will lie in the interval $(-1.96, 1.96).$

Now, here's the trick. We solve the inequality inside the parentheses of the last probability statement for the population mean $\mu\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-1.96< & \,Z<1.96 \\ -1.96< & \,\frac{\overset{―}{x}-\mu }{\sigma /\sqrt{n}}<1.96 \\ -1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}< & \,\overset{―}{x}-\mu <1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}} \\ -\overset{―}{x}-1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}< & \,-\mu \,<-\overset{―}{x}+1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}} \\ \overset{―}{x}+1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}> & \,\mu >\overset{―}{x}-1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}} \\ \overset{―}{x}-1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}< & \,\mu <\overset{―}{x}+1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu$ is given by

$$
\left(\overline{x} - 1.96\cdot\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}},\: \overline{x} + 1.96\cdot\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)
$$

Finally, substituting our values

$$
n=10, \qquad
\overline{x}=12, \qquad
\sigma=3,
$$

we obtain that our $95\%$ confidence interval for $\mu$ is 

$$
\big( 12- 1.859, \: 12 + 1.859 \big).
$$

 

Now that we've seen how to construct a particular confidence interval, let's discuss the more general procedure."] [17592186060967 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population with the unknown population mean $\mu$ and *known* population variance $\sigma^2.$ Then, for a given value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1,$ a $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu$ is given by

$$
\left(\overline{x} - z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}, \: \overline{x} + z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)
$$

where $P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},$ and $Z \sim N(0,1).$ 

The endpoints of our confidence interval are called **confidence limits** and are given by

$$
\overline{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

Each part of the formula above has a name:

- $\overline{x}$ is an estimate of the population mean

- $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ is the standard error of the mean

- $z_{\alpha/2}$ is the corresponding $z$-score

- $E = z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ is the margin of error

![](images/58/581fc2da88e4419e78389a1b5eedb127f590641d0b7ee21c489ed85184795b13.svg)

So, our confidence interval can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\overset{―}{x}-[\text{margin of error}], & \,\overset{―}{x}+[\text{margin of error}]) \\ (\overset{―}{x}-[\text{[math]z[/math]-score}]\cdot [\text{standard error}], & \,\overset{―}{x}+[\text{[math]z[/math]-score}]\cdot [\text{standard error}]) \\ (\overset{―}{x}-{z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}, & \,\overset{―}{x}+{z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}})\end{aligned}
$$

Since computing a confidence interval amounts to finding the corresponding confidence limits, we will use the two terms interchangeably."] [17592186060966 :tutorial/content "It's important to be able to interpret confidence intervals correctly.

Imagine we conduct several independent random samples from a population. The mean of the sample will be different for each sample. Some values of $\overline{x}$ might lie close to the population mean $\mu,$ and some could lie further away.

Suppose we construct a $90\%$ confidence interval for each sample and plot them on the same diagram. We might get a picture similar to the one below.

![](images/fc/fc8dd707751cd9e1cb0da1bf618b6d7aed740fab875d8d49c7c89fc09b77321e.png)

In the diagram above, we see that nine out of ten of our confidence intervals contain $\mu,$ while one of them (the red one) does *not* contain the population mean $\mu.$ 

The idea is that if we construct many $90\%$ confidence intervals, one for each sample, then approximately $90\%$ of these confidence intervals will contain the population mean $\mu.$"] [17592186060965 :tutorial/content "Up to now, we've assumed that the underlying population is normally distributed. $$

$$
\begin{aligned}Y & ={a}_{1}{X}_{1}+{a}_{2}{X}_{2}+{a}_{3}{X}_{3} \\  & ∼N({a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3},\,{a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have

$$
X_1\sim N(4,5), \qquad
X_2\sim N(-2,2), \qquad
X_3\sim N(3,1),
$$

and

$$
Y=3X_1-3X_2-X_3.
$$

Since $X_1, X_2,$ and $X_3$ are mutually independent, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3} \\  & =3\cdot 4+(-3)\cdot (-2)+(-1)\cdot 3 \\  & =15, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2} \\  & ={3}^{2}\cdot 5+(-3)^{2}\cdot 2+(-1)^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =9\cdot 5+9\cdot 2+1\cdot 1 \\  & =64.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}Y∼N(15,64).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(|Y |\lt  3)=P(-3 <  Y \lt  3).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-3<Y<3) & =P(\frac{-3-15}{\sqrt{64}}<Z<\frac{3-15}{\sqrt{64}}) \\  & ≈P(-2.25<Z<-1.5) \\  & =P(Z<-1.5)-P(Z<-2.25) \\  & =Φ(-1.5)-Φ(-2.25)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-1.5)≈0.0668,\,Φ(-2.25)≈0.0122.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|Y|<3) & =Φ(-1.5)-Φ(-2.25) \\  & ≈0.0668-0.0122 \\  & =0.0546.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186175686 :question/problem "A shop sells $2$ types of rice, Type $A$ and Type $B.$ The volume per packet for Type $A$ rice is normally distributed with a mean of $1$ liter and a variance of $0.01$ liters2, while the volume per packet for Type $B$ rice is normally distributed with a mean of $0.7$ liters and a variance of $0.02$ liters2. $$

$$

Let the random variable $Y$ denote the total resulting volume of rice after cooking. Since the Type $A$ rice quadruples in volume, while the type $B$ rice triples in volume, we have

$$
Y= 4X_1+3X_2 + 3X_3.
$$

The random variable $Y$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =(4\cdot 1+3\cdot 0.7+3\cdot 0.7) \\  & =8.2 \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={4}^{2}\cdot 0.01+{3}^{2}\cdot 0.02+{3}^{2}\cdot 0.02 \\  & =16\cdot 0.01+9\cdot 0.02+9\cdot 0.02 \\  & =0.52.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<8) & =P(Z<\frac{8-8.2}{\sqrt{0.52}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<-0.28) \\  & =Φ(-0.28)\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<8) & ≈Φ(-0.28) \\  & ≈0.3897.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-d6053da2-f1d5-5511-b304-aa8032f24e40" :question/id #uuid "d6053da2-f1d5-5511-b304-aa8032f24e40"] ["question-d6053da2-f1d5-5511-b304-aa8032f24e40" :question/math-academy-id "q-142941"] ["question-d6053da2-f1d5-5511-b304-aa8032f24e40" :question/problem "Given that the random variables

$$
{X}_{1}∼N({\mu }_{1},{\sigma }_{1}^{2}),\,{X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N({\mu }_{3},{\sigma }_{3}^{2}),
$$

then 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y & ={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+{X}_{3} \\  & ∼N({\mu }_{1}+{\mu }_{2}+{\mu }_{3},\,{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{\sigma }_{3}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(0,{3}^{2}),\,{X}_{2}∼N(3,{2}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N(1,{2}^{2}),
$$

and

$$
Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+{X}_{3}.
$$

Since ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ are mutually independent, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\mu }_{1}+{\mu }_{2}+{\mu }_{3} \\  & =0+3+1 \\  & =4, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{\sigma }_{3}^{2} \\  & ={3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2} \\  & =9+4+4 \\  & =17.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+{X}_{3} & ∼N(4,17).\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-c3a863b6-3f9a-5678-9da7-4af2ad4a2999" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-47a3d4eb-cdba-5f52-b2b1-08d4c2047e6b" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
{X}_{1}∼N(-1,3),\,{X}_{2}∼N(3,2),\,{X}_{3}∼N(1,1)
$$

are mutually independent, what is the distribution of $Y=3{X}_{1}-4{X}_{2}-2{X}_{3}?$"] ["question-2c34156c-74ee-5271-a0cf-be78f0930f45" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ are mutually independent random variables, where 

$$
{X}_{1}∼N({\mu }_{1},{\sigma }_{1}^{2}),\,{X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N({\mu }_{3},{\sigma }_{3}^{2}),
$$

and ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are real constants,  then 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y & ={a}_{1}{X}_{1}+{a}_{2}{X}_{2}+{a}_{3}{X}_{3} \\  & ∼N({a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3},\,{a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(-1,3),\,{X}_{2}∼N(3,2),\,{X}_{3}∼N(1,1),
$$

and

$$
Y=3{X}_{1}-4{X}_{2}-2{X}_{3}.
$$

Since ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ are mutually independent, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3} \\  & =3\cdot (-1)+(-4)\cdot 3+(-2)\cdot 1 \\  & =-3-12-2 \\  & =-17, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2} \\  & ={3}^{2}\cdot 3+(-4)^{2}\cdot 2+(-2)^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =9\cdot 3+16\cdot 2+4\cdot 1 \\  & =27+32+4 \\  & =63.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y=3{X}_{1}-4{X}_{2}-2{X}_{3} & ∼N(-17,63).\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-2c34156c-74ee-5271-a0cf-be78f0930f45" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-16afd0ce-a98f-530b-911d-c450c3840e38" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3} \\  & =3\cdot 3+1\cdot 2+2\cdot 6 \\  & =23 \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2} \\  & ={3}^{2}\cdot {5}^{2}+{1}^{2}\cdot 15+{2}^{2}\cdot {2}^{2} \\  & =9\cdot 25+1\cdot 15+4\cdot 4 \\  & =256.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}Y∼N(23,256).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<43) & =P(Z<\frac{43-23}{\sqrt{256}}) \\  & =P(Z<1.25) \\  & =Φ(1.25)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
Φ(1.25)≈0.8944.
$$

$$
{X}_{1}∼N({\mu }_{1},{\sigma }_{1}^{2}),\,{X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N({\mu }_{3},{\sigma }_{3}^{2}),
$$

and ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are real constants,  then 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y & ={a}_{1}{X}_{1}+{a}_{2}{X}_{2}+{a}_{3}{X}_{3} \\  & ∼N({a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3},\,{a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(2,2),\,{X}_{2}∼N(1,{3}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N(3,8),
$$

and

$$
Y=4{X}_{1}+3{X}_{2}-{X}_{3}.
$$

Since ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ are mutually independent, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3} \\  & =4\cdot 2+3\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 3 \\  & =8, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2} \\  & ={4}^{2}\cdot 2+{3}^{2}\cdot {3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}\cdot 8 \\  & =16\cdot 2+9\cdot 9+1\cdot 8 \\  & =121.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}Y∼N(8,121).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(5<Y<10).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(5<Y<10) & =P(\frac{5-8}{\sqrt{121}}<Z<\frac{10-8}{\sqrt{121}}) \\  & ≈P(-0.27<Z<0.18) \\  & =P(Z<0.18)-P(Z<-0.27) \\  & =Φ(0.18)-Φ(-0.27)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.27)≈0.3936,\,Φ(0.18)≈0.5714.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(5<Y<10) & =Φ(0.18)-Φ(-0.27) \\  & ≈0.5714-0.3936 \\  & =0.1778.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-fef171e3-d5a0-5ed0-9b02-411a8ba77086" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-83ab6bc9-a41c-5d82-bfee-b7f11dd65ee3" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
{X}_{1}∼N({\mu }_{1},{\sigma }_{1}^{2}),\,{X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N({\mu }_{3},{\sigma }_{3}^{2}),
$$

and ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are real constants,  then 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y & ={a}_{1}{X}_{1}+{a}_{2}{X}_{2}+{a}_{3}{X}_{3} \\  & ∼N({a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3},\,{a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(5,1),\,{X}_{2}∼N(8,14),\,{X}_{3}∼N(1,2),
$$

and

$$
Y=4{X}_{1}+2{X}_{2}+6{X}_{3}.
$$

Since ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ are mutually independent, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3} \\  & =4\cdot 5+2\cdot 8+6\cdot 1 \\  & =42, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2} \\  & ={4}^{2}\cdot 1+{2}^{2}\cdot 14+{6}^{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =16\cdot 1+4\cdot 14+36\cdot 2 \\  & =144.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}Y∼N(42,144).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(|Y|>1).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|Y|>1) & =P(Y<-1)+P(Y>1) \\  & =P(Z<\frac{-1-42}{\sqrt{144}})+P(Z>\frac{1-42}{\sqrt{144}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<-3.58)+P(Z>-3.42) \\  & =P(Z<-3.58)+(1-P(Z<-3.42)) \\  & =1+Φ(-3.58)-Φ(-3.42)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-3.58)≈0.0002,\,Φ(-3.42)≈0.0003.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|Y|>1) & =1+Φ(-3.58)-Φ(-3.42) \\  & ≈1+0.0002-0.0003 \\  & =0.9999.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-29e90455-0d48-5325-bbcb-97a6b476016a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-2a370832-b0c9-5295-a560-27c242048c60" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-1ed551ba-20e8-589e-8222-2bcdb2f9bd69" :question/math-academy-id "q-143228"] ["question-1ed551ba-20e8-589e-8222-2bcdb2f9bd69" :question/problem "Given that the random variables 

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(-1,7),\,{X}_{2}∼N(3,2),\,{X}_{3}∼N(5,9)
$$

are mutually independent and $Y={X}_{1}-3{X}_{2}+4{X}_{3},$ calculate $P(Y>22).$ 

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.7\,$ | $\,0.7580\,$ | $\,0.7611\,$ | $\,0.7642\,$ | $\,0.7673\,$ |

| $\,0.9\,$ | $\,0.8159\,$ | $\,0.8186\,$ | $\,0.8212\,$ | $\,0.8238\,$ |
| $\,1.0\,$ | $\,0.8413\,$ | $\,0.8438\,$ | $\,0.8461\,$ | $\,0.8485\,$ |"] ["question-1ed551ba-20e8-589e-8222-2bcdb2f9bd69" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ are mutually independent random variables, where 

$$
{X}_{1}∼N({\mu }_{1},{\sigma }_{1}^{2}),\,{X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N({\mu }_{3},{\sigma }_{3}^{2}),
$$

and ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are real constants,  then 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y & ={a}_{1}{X}_{1}+{a}_{2}{X}_{2}+{a}_{3}{X}_{3} \\  & ∼N({a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3},\,{a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(-1,7),\,{X}_{2}∼N(3,2),\,{X}_{3}∼N(5,9),
$$

and

$$
Y={X}_{1}-3{X}_{2}+4{X}_{3}.
$$

Since ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ are mutually independent, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)+(-3)\cdot 3+4\cdot 5 \\  & =10 \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2} \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot 7+(-3)^{2}\cdot 2+{4}^{2}\cdot 9 \\  & =1\cdot 7+9\cdot 2+16\cdot 9 \\  & =169.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}Y∼N(10,169).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(Y>22).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y>22) & =P(Z>\frac{22-10}{\sqrt{169}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>0.92) \\  & =1-P(Z<0.92) \\  & =1-Φ(0.92)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(0.92)≈0.8212.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y>22) & =1-Φ(0.92) \\  & =1-0.8212 \\  & ≈0.1788.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-1ed551ba-20e8-589e-8222-2bcdb2f9bd69" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-ab1f8fdc-9fb8-59c9-89bb-5d70cfa1beab" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
{X}_{1}∼N({\mu }_{1},{\sigma }_{1}^{2}),\,{X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N({\mu }_{3},{\sigma }_{3}^{2}),
$$

and ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are real constants,  then 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y & ={a}_{1}{X}_{1}+{a}_{2}{X}_{2}+{a}_{3}{X}_{3} \\  & ∼N({a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3},\,{a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(7,15),\,{X}_{2}∼N(-2,5),\,{X}_{3}∼N(12,16),
$$

and

$$
Y=-{X}_{1}-{X}_{2}-{X}_{3}.
$$

Since ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ are mutually independent, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3} \\  & =(-1)\cdot 7+(-1)\cdot (-2)+(-1)\cdot 12 \\  & =-17, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2} \\  & =(-1)^{2}\cdot 15+(-1)^{2}\cdot 5+(-1)^{2}\cdot 16 \\  & =15+5+16 \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}Y∼N(-17,36).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(|Y|<6)=P(-6<Y<6).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-6<Y<6) & =P(\frac{-6-(-17)}{\sqrt{36}}<Z<\frac{6-(-17)}{\sqrt{36}}) \\  & ≈P(1.83<Z<3.83) \\  & =P(Z<3.83)-P(Z<1.83) \\  & =Φ(3.83)-Φ(1.83)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(3.83)≈0.9999,\,Φ(1.83)≈0.9664.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|Y|<6) & =Φ(3.83)-Φ(1.83) \\  & ≈0.9999-0.9664 \\  & =0.0335.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-7f3eef4b-44d7-5d7f-9ad0-9c61a5d17d35" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-bfedd8c4-3438-59cf-b82a-4a4b574ae14b" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-64b4d9dd-0ca6-5664-aa15-145818c765b0" :question/math-academy-id "q-143245"] ["question-64b4d9dd-0ca6-5664-aa15-145818c765b0" :question/problem "The volumes of some chocolate muffins before cooking are normally distributed with a mean of $57\,\text{ml}$ and a standard deviation of $2\,\text{ml}.$
In contrast, the volumes of some pumpkin muffins before cooking are normally distributed with a mean of $42\,\text{ml}$ and a standard deviation of $1\,\text{ml},$ while the volumes of some blueberry muffins before cooking are normally distributed with a mean of $48\,\text{ml}$ and a standard deviation of $1.5\,\text{ml}.$
During cooking, it is known that chocolate muffins double in volume, while pumpkin and blueberry muffins triple in volume.

If a chocolate muffin, a  pumpkin muffin, and a blueberry muffin are randomly selected after cooking, what is the probability that the sum of their volumes is less than $400\,\text{ml}?$ You may assume that the volumes of the muffins are independent. 

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ | $\,0.09\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,2.1\,$ | $\,0.9842\,$ | $\,0.9846\,$ | $\,0.9850\,$ | $\,0.9854\,$ | $\,0.9857\,$ |
| $\,2.2\,$ | $\,0.9878\,$ | $\,0.9881\,$ | $\,0.9884\,$ | $\,0.9887\,$ | $\,0.9890\,$ |
| $\,2.3\,$ | $\,0.9906\,$ | $\,0.9909\,$ | $\,0.9911\,$ | $\,0.9913\,$ | $\,0.9916\,$ |"] ["question-64b4d9dd-0ca6-5664-aa15-145818c765b0" :question/worked-solution "Let ${X}_{1}$, ${X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ denote the volume of the chocolate, the pumpkin, and the blueberry muffins, respectively. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(57,{2}^{2}),\,{X}_{2}∼N(42,{1}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N(48,{1.5}^{2}).
$$

Let the random variable $Y$ denote the total volume of the randomly selected chocolate, pumpkin, and blueberry muffins after cooking. Since the chocolate muffin doubled in volume, while the pumpkin and blueberry muffins tripled in volume during cooking, we have

$$
Y=2{X}_{1}+3{X}_{2}+3{X}_{3}.
$$

The random variable $Y$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =(2\cdot 57+3\cdot 42+3\cdot 48) \\  & =384 \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={2}^{2}\cdot {2}^{2}+{3}^{2}\cdot {1}^{2}+{3}^{2}\cdot {1.5}^{2} \\  & =4\cdot 4+9\cdot 1+9\cdot 2.25 \\  & =45.25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
Y∼N(384,45.25).
$$

In order to find $P(Y<400),$ we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<400) & =P(Z<\frac{400-384}{\sqrt{45.25}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<2.38) \\  & =Φ(2.38)\end{aligned}
$$

["question-dd5e602a-e46f-521b-9487-8ddb9d6bb489" :question/math-academy-id "q-143246"] ["question-dd5e602a-e46f-521b-9487-8ddb9d6bb489" :question/problem "The weights of some chocolate cookies are normally distributed with a mean of $10\,\text{g}$ and a variance of $1\,{\text{g}}^{2}.$
On the other hand, the weights of some oatcakes are normally distributed with a mean of $15\,\text{g}$ and a variance of $2\,{\text{g}}^{2},$ while the weights of some macaroons are normally distributed with a mean of $14\,\text{g}$ and a variance of $1.5\,{\text{g}}^{2}.$ 

If one chocolate cookie, one oatcake, and one macaroon are randomly selected, what is the probability that the sum of $6$ times the weight of the cookie and $5$ times the weight of the oatcake is less than $10$ times the weight of the macaroon? You may assume that the weights are independent. 

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.1\,$ | $\,0.5398\,$ | $\,0.5438\,$ | $\,0.5478\,$ | $\,0.5517\,$ | $\,0.5557\,$ |
| $\,0.2\,$ | $\,0.5793\,$ | $\,0.5832\,$ | $\,0.5871\,$ | $\,0.5910\,$ | $\,0.5948\,$ |
| $\,0.3\,$ | $\,0.6179\,$ | $\,0.6217\,$ | $\,0.6255\,$ | $\,0.6293\,$ | $\,0.6331\,$ |"] ["question-dd5e602a-e46f-521b-9487-8ddb9d6bb489" :question/worked-solution "Let ${X}_{1}$, ${X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ denote the weight of the chocolate cookie, the oatcake, and the macaroon, respectively. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(10,1),\,{X}_{2}∼N(15,2),\,{X}_{3}∼N(14,1.5).
$$

Let the random variable $Y$ denote the difference between the sum of $6$ times the weight of the cookie and $5$ times the weight of the oatcake, and $10$ times the weight of the macaroon. Then, we have $Y=6{X}_{1}+5{X}_{2}-10{X}_{3},$ and we want to find 

$$
P(Y<0).
$$

The random variable $Y$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =(6\cdot 10+4\cdot 15-10\cdot 14) \\  & =-5 \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={6}^{2}\cdot 1+{5}^{2}\cdot 2+{10}^{2}\cdot 1.5 \\  & =36+50+150 \\  & =236.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
Y∼N(-5,236).
$$

In order to find $P(Y<0),$ we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<0) & =P(Z<\frac{0-(-5)}{\sqrt{236}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<0.33) \\  & =Φ(0.33)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(0.33)≈0.6293.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<0) & ≈Φ(0.33) \\  & ≈0.6293.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-dd5e602a-e46f-521b-9487-8ddb9d6bb489" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-b2c45f73-b1f8-512b-9418-cf6c5cfb2517" :answer-field/id #uuid *Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $\,1.2\,$ | $\,0.8849\,$ | $\,0.8869\,$ | $\,0.8888\,$ | $\,0.8907\,$ | $\,0.8925\,$ | $\,0.8944\,$ |
| $\,1.3\,$ | $\,0.9032\,$ | $\,0.9049\,$ | $\,0.9066\,$ | $\,0.9082\,$ | $\,0.9099\,$ | $\,0.9115\,$ |"] ["question-78e73be3-8be0-5432-b894-38767fce09cc" :question/worked-solution "Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ denote the length of the three tubes, respectively. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(6,{0.1}^{2}),\,{X}_{2}∼N(6,{0.1}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N(6,{0.1}^{2}).
$$

Let the random variable $Y$ denote the total length of the tubes. Then, we have

$$
Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+{X}_{3}.
$$

The random variable $Y$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =3\cdot 6 \\  & =18, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={0.1}^{2}+{0.1}^{2}+{0.1}^{2} \\  & =0.03.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
Y∼N(18,0.03).
$$

In order to find $P(Y>18.2),$ we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y>18.2) & =P(Z>\frac{18.2-18}{\sqrt{0.03}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>1.15) \\  & =1-P(Z<1.15) \\  & =1-Φ(1.15)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(1.15)≈0.8749.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y>18.2) & ≈=1-Φ(1.15) \\  & ≈1-0.8749 \\  & =0.1251.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-78e73be3-8be0-5432-b894-38767fce09cc" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-951f3143-eda4-58c8-bc35-b4c51724f1fd" :answer-field/id #uuid | $\,0.8\,$ | $\,0.7881\,$ | $\,0.7910\,$ | $\,0.7939\,$ | $\,0.7967\,$ | $\,0.7995\,$ |"] ["question-4a63a0a4-bc99-5394-8795-605d4e119f34" :question/worked-solution "Let ${X}_{1}$, ${X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ denote the student's math, science, and language test results, respectively. Then, we have

$$
Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+{X}_{3}.
$$

The random variable $Y$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =(70+65+55) \\  & =190, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={6}^{2}+{10}^{2}+{15}^{2} \\  & =36+100+225 \\  & =361.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
Y∼N(190,361).

In order to find $P(Y>200),$ we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y>200) & =P(Z>\frac{200-190}{\sqrt{361}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>0.53) \\  & =1-P(Z<0.53) \\  & =1-Φ(0.53)\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y>200) & ≈1-Φ(0.53) \\  & ≈1-0.7019 \\  & =0.2981.\end{aligned}

"question-4a63a0a4-bc99-5394-8795-605d4e119f34"] [17592186176289 :question/problem "A course grade is calculated by adding the results of a written test, oral test, and colloquium, contributing $50%$, $30%,$ and $20%,$ respectively to the final grade. 

The written test results are normally distributed with a mean of $64$ and a standard deviation of $8.$ The oral test results are normally distributed with a mean of $50$ and a standard deviation of $10$, while the results of the colloquium are normally distributed with a mean of $60$ and a standard deviation of $10.$ Find the probability that a randomly selected student achieves a grade greater than $70.$ You may assume that the scores on each test are independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,1.9\,$ | $\,0.9713\,$ | $\,0.9719\,$ | $\,0.9726\,$ | $\,0.9732\,$ | $\,0.9738\,$ |
| $\,2.0\,$ | $\,0.9772\,$ | $\,0.9778\,$ | $\,0.9783\,$ | $\,0.9788\,$ | $\,0.9793\,$ |
| $\,2.1\,$ | $\,0.9821\,$ | $\,0.9826\,$ | $\,0.9830\,$ | $\,0.9834\,$ | $\,0.9838\,$ |"] [17592186176289 :question/worked-solution "Let ${X}_{1}$, ${X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ denote the written test, oral test, and colloquium results, respectively. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(64,{8}^{2}),\,{X}_{2}∼N(50,{10}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N(60,{10}^{2}).
$$

Let the random variable $Y$ denote the final grade of a randomly selected student. Since the written, oral, and colloquium contribute $50%$, $30%,$ and $20%$, respectively, to the final grade, we have

$$
Y=0.5{X}_{1}+0.3{X}_{2}+0.2{X}_{3}.
$$

The random variable $Y$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =0.5\cdot 64+0.3\cdot 50+0.2\cdot 60 \\  & =59, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & =(0.5)^{2}\cdot {8}^{2}+(0.3)^{2}\cdot {10}^{2}+(0.2)^{2}\cdot {10}^{2} \\  & =0.25\cdot 64+0.09\cdot 10+0.04\cdot 100 \\  & =29.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}Y & ∼N(59,29).\end{aligned}
$$

In order to find $P(Y>70),$ we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y>70) & =P(Z>\frac{70-59}{\sqrt{29}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>2.04) \\  & =1-P(Z<2.04) \\  & =1-Φ(2.04)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(2.04)≈0.9793.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y>70) & ≈1-Φ(2.04) \\  & ≈1-0.9793 \\  & =0.0207.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186176289 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] [17592186173992 :answer-field/correct 17592186173997] [17592186177055 :tutorial/content "When we form a random variable $Y$ from a sum of **mutually independent**, normally distributed random variables, the distribution of $Y$ is also normal.

More precisely, we have the following theorem:

*If $X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n$ are mutually independent normal random variables such that*

$$
X_1 \sim N(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2), \qquad X_2\sim (\mu_2,\sigma_2^2), \qquad \ldots, \quad X_n\sim(\mu_n,\sigma_n^2),
$$

 

*then the random variable* 

$$
Y=X_1+X_2+\ldots+X_n
$$

 

*is normally distributed, where*

$$
Y\sim N(\mu_1+\mu_2+\ldots+\mu_n, \: \sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2+\ldots+\sigma_n^2).
$$

For example, if the random variables

$$
X_1\sim N({\color{blue}2},{\color{red}3}), \qquad X_2\sim  N({\color{blue}1},{\color{red}4}), \qquad X_3\sim N({\color{blue}1},{\color{red}1})
$$

are mutually independent, then 

$$
Y=X_1+X_2+X_3
$$

is normally distributed. 

Let's figure out the distribution of $Y.$ We start by computing its mean and variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\mu }_{1}+{\mu }_{2}+{\mu }_{3} \\  & =2+1+1 \\  & =4, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{\sigma }_{3}^{2} \\  & =3+4+1 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+{X}_{3} & ∼N(4,8).\end{aligned}
$$

**Watch out!** It is vital that $X_1, X_2,\ldots X_n$ are *mutually independent*."] [17592186177005 :tutorial/content "When we form a random variable $Y$ from a linear combination of mutually independent, normally distributed random variables, the distribution of $Y$ is also normal.

Y\sim N(a_1\mu_1+a_2\mu_2+\ldots+a_n\mu_n, \: a_1^2\sigma_1^2+a_2^2\sigma_2^2+\ldots+a_n^2\sigma_n^2).

$$

are mutually independent, then 

$$
Y= \bbox[2pt,AntiqueWhite]{3}X_1+\bbox[2pt,AntiqueWhite]{2}X_2+\bbox[2pt,AntiqueWhite]{4}X_3
$$

is normally distributed. 

Let's figure out the distribution of $Y.$ We start by computing its mean and variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3} \\  & =3\cdot 2+2\cdot 1+4\cdot 1 \\  & =6+2+4 \\  & =12, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2} \\  & ={3}^{2}\cdot 3+{2}^{2}\cdot 4+{4}^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =9\cdot 3+4\cdot 4+16\cdot 1 \\  & =27+16+16 \\  & =59.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Y=3{X}_{1}+2{X}_{2}+4{X}_{3} & ∼N(12,59).\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate ${∮}_{∂D}x\,dy-y\,dx,$ where $D$ is the region shown above."] [17592186134097 :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}x\,dy-y\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-(-1))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =2\cdot ({4}^{2}-{2}^{2}) \\  & =2\cdot (16-4) \\  & =2\cdot 12 \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186134097 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] [17592186130738 :answer-field/correct 17592186130739] ["question-e2260d96-b984-5295-801c-28a9593008a3" :question/id #uuid "e2260d96-b984-5295-801c-28a9593008a3"] ["question-e2260d96-b984-5295-801c-28a9593008a3" :question/math-academy-id "q-126851"] ["question-e2260d96-b984-5295-801c-28a9593008a3" :question/problem "![](images/e9/e9892ef4efa3481ad02f7b8e38f1bae1876b196627204521d011656010297281.png)

Suppose that $F$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ defined over the region $D$ above. Given that 

$$
{∮}_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=16,\,{∮}_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=6,\,{∮}_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r=4,
$$

where ${C}_{1}$ is oriented counterclockwise and ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ are oriented clockwise, calculate the value of ${∮}_{∂D}F\cdot \text{d}r.$"] ["question-e2260d96-b984-5295-801c-28a9593008a3" :question/worked-solution "To calculate the total circulation of a vector field over the boundary of a region containing holes, we add together the circulations over each *positively oriented* boundary.

Remember that:

- the positive direction is *counterclockwise* for the *outer* curve ${C}_{1}$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse ${C}_{1}$ counterclockwise), and

- the positive direction is *clockwise* for the *inner* curves ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ clockwise).

The diagram below shows the positive orientations of all three curves.

![](images/b2/b20b2b911c2a417c26fa951d9b28efa296c265df25e9d06b635ef4846267b93b.png)

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={∮}_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{∮}_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{∮}_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =16+6+4 \\  & =26.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-e2260d96-b984-5295-801c-28a9593008a3" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-a7d01b58-0857-54fb-bdf6-61d33e711eeb" :answer-field/id #uuid Calculate ${∮}_{∂D}(1-4y)\,dx+(2+5x)\,dy,$ where $D$ is the annular region shown above."] ["question-09c35a82-4469-5857-aed4-331c374b8ab3" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=1-4y$ and $Q(x,y)=2+5x.$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-4,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=5.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}dx+x\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(5-(-4))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}9\,\text{d}A \\  & =9\,\text{Area}(D) \\  & =9\cdot (\pi \cdot {3}^{2}-\pi \cdot {2}^{2}) \\  & =9\cdot 5\pi  \\  & =45\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-09c35a82-4469-5857-aed4-331c374b8ab3" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-30362ef7-7428-53da-a7f2-7fe7cc3d3d5c" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-700640db-e0fe-571f-9cca-6b3afdd864a7"] [17592186153338 :tutorial/content "How does a proportional relationship look when we plot it in the $(x,y)$ plane?

To answer this, let's consider the following proportional relationship:

$$
y = 2x
$$

To plot a graph, we first need a table of values. 

| $x$ | $y$ |
| --- | --- |
| $0$ |  |
| $1$ |  |
| $2$ |  |
| $3$ |  |

Filling in the $y$-values using the equation $y = 2x,$ we get the following:

| $x$ | $y$ |
| --- | --- |
| $0$ | $0$ |
| $1$ | $2$ |
| $2$ | $4$ |
| $3$ | $6$ |

So, we have the following $(x,y)$ coordinates:

$$
(0,0), \quad (1,2),  \quad (2,4),  \quad (3,6)
$$

If we plot these points in the coordinate plane, we get the following:

![](images/a8/a8cd951c66c67b8f28b791011c7553675b3112029d9ebe4b19769127b5e75bd5.png)

This leads us to the following important fact:

*The graph of any proportional relationship is a straight line that passes through the origin $(0,0)$.*"] [17592186153339 :tutorial/content "When there is a proportional relationship between $x$ and $y,$ we can express this using the **proportionality symbol** $\propto,$ as follows:

$$
y \propto x
$$

Note that the following statements are all equivalent:

- $y = kx$

- $y$ **varies directly** with $x$

- $y$ is **directly proportional** to $x$

- $y \propto x$"] [17592186152310 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] ["question-556e4e71-69c2-58ca-8978-843d74c13525" :question/id #uuid "556e4e71-69c2-58ca-8978-843d74c13525"] ["question-556e4e71-69c2-58ca-8978-843d74c13525" :question/math-academy-id "q-132102"] ["question-556e4e71-69c2-58ca-8978-843d74c13525" :question/problem "Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ where $F(x,y,z)=4xy\,i+(2{x}^{2}+2yz)\,j+({y}^{2}+1)\,k.$"] ["question-556e4e71-69c2-58ca-8978-843d74c13525" :question/worked-solution "The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,k.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=4xy,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}+2yz,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}+1
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 4xy\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{x}^{2}y+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}+2yz$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2{x}^{2}+2yz \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2yz\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int 2yz\,\text{d}y \\  & ={y}^{2}z+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)={y}^{2}z+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=2{x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}+1$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+1 & ={y}^{2}+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =1 \\ h(z) & =z+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=2{x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+z+C.
$$"] ["question-556e4e71-69c2-58ca-8978-843d74c13525" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-2575d212-1190-514e-a919-fd516555543d" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Let the function $f(x,y)$ be defined as

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}{y}^{2},\, & \text{if}\,-1<x<1,\,0<y<2, \\ {2}^{xy},\, & \text{if}\,1<x<3,\,0<y<2.\end{aligned}

{∬}_{(-1,3)\times (0,2)}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=
$$"] ["question-0c17f34a-606d-54c2-a49c-4cce7dcaf8e5" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that the rectangle $R$ can be represented as a union of two smaller rectangles, as follows:  

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =((-1,1)\cup (1,3))\times (0,2) \\  & =((-1,1)\times (0,2))\cup ((1,3)\times (0,2)).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1\},
$$

$$
T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)),

- The operation ${R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}$ involves swapping two rows, so it changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite one.

- The operation ${R}_{3}:=4{R}_{3}$ involves multiplying a row by $4,$ so the determinant is multiplied by $4$ as well.

Therefore, we have to change the sign of the determinant to the opposite one and multiply by $4$ as well. Consequently, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B) & =4\cdot (-det(A)) \\  & =-4det(A) \\  & =-4\cdot 6 \\  & =-24.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-023c52b0-f119-5895-8d3f-31a9468a20b5" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-594aa2c5-6ab3-59e0-94ef-12b55bd75a5d" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-ba829ff8-bbca-5643-baef-27f89f8dddf9" :question/problem "Find the center and radius of the circle whose equation is ${x}^{2}+6x+{y}^{2}=40.$"] ["question-ba829ff8-bbca-5643-baef-27f89f8dddf9" :question/worked-solution "To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+6x+{y}^{2} & =40 \\ ({x}^{2}+6x)+{y}^{2} & =40 \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2})+{y}^{2} & =40+{3}^{2} \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2})+{y}^{2} & =49\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2}+(y-0)^{2} & ={7}^{2} \\ (x-(-3))^{2}+(y-0)^{2} & ={7}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the circle is centered at $(-3,0)$ and its radius is $7.$"] ["question-ba829ff8-bbca-5643-baef-27f89f8dddf9" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 & 1 \\ 3 & 8 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 8 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -11 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}-11 & 3 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}].

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}-11 & 3 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-1)\cdot (-11)-4\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ -4 & -11\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 4 & 11\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

	}

$$

$$

$$
