I.I.D random variables, where

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(5,{2}^{2}),\,1\le i\le 14,
$$

calculate $P(70\le Y\le 78),$ where  $Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{14}.$

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,1.0\,$ | $\,0.8531\,$ | $\,0.8554\,$ | $\,0.8577\,$ | $\,0.8599\,$ |
| $\,1.1\,$ | $\,0.8749\,$ | $\,0.8770\,$ | $\,0.8790\,$ | $\,0.8810\,$ |
| $\,1.2\,$ | $\,0.8944\,$ | $\,0.8962\,$ | $\,0.8980\,$ | $\,0.8997\,$ |"] ["question-2bacd74e-2117-5657-b43b-3639319ee133" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed (I.I.D) normal random variables, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then 

$$
Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{n}∼N(n\mu ,\,n{\sigma }^{2}).
$$

Therefore, since ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{14}$ are independent and identically distributed, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{14} & ∼N(14\cdot 5,\,14\cdot {2}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(14\cdot 5,\,14\cdot 4) \\  & =N(70,56).\end{aligned}
$$

We wish to compute the probability $P(70\le Y\le 78).$ We first convert $Y$ into a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(70\le Y\le 78) & =P(\frac{70-70}{\sqrt{56}}\le Z\le \frac{78-70}{\sqrt{56}}) \\  & =P(0\le Z\le \frac{8}{\sqrt{56}}) \\  & =P(0\le Z\le 1.07) \\  & =Φ(1.07)-Φ(0) \\  & =Φ(1.07)-0.5\end{aligned}
$$

From the $z$-table, we have

$$
Φ(1.07)=0.8577.
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(70\le Y\le 78)=Φ(1.07)-0.5=0.8577-0.5=0.3577.
$$"] ["question-2bacd74e-2117-5657-b43b-3639319ee133" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-cffd4deb-f454-53d3-9291-7403d64f70f3" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Given that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{18}$ are I.I.D random variables, where

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(1,{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2}),\,1\le i\le 18,
$$

calculate $P(16\le Y\le 20),$ where  $Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{18}.$

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.5\,$ | $\,0.7088\,$ | $\,0.7123\,$ | $\,0.7157\,$ | $\,0.7190\,$ |
| $\,0.6\,$ | $\,0.7422\,$ | $\,0.7454\,$ | $\,0.7486\,$ | $\,0.7517\,$ |
| $\,0.7\,$ | $\,0.7734\,$ | $\,0.7764\,$ | $\,0.7794\,$ | $\,0.7823\,$ |"] ["question-4bd1cff1-6c69-5338-8c54-dfce19778dbc" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed (I.I.D) normal random variables, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then 

$$
Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{n}∼N(n\mu ,\,n{\sigma }^{2}).
$$

Therefore, since ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{18}$ are independent and identically distributed, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{18} & ∼N(18\cdot 1,\,18\cdot {(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(18\cdot 1,\,18\cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =N(18,9).\end{aligned}
$$

We wish to compute the probability $P(16\le Y\le 20).$ We first convert $Y$ into a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(16\le Y\le 20) & =P(\frac{16-18}{\sqrt{9}}\le Z\le \frac{20-18}{\sqrt{9}}) \\  & =P(-\frac{2}{3}\le Z\le \frac{2}{3}) \\  & ≈P(-0.67\le Z\le 0.67) \\  & =1-2P(Z\ge 0.67) \\  & =1-2(1-P(Z\le 0.67)) \\  & =2P(Z\le 0.67))-1 \\  & =2Φ(0.67)-1\end{aligned}
$$

From the $z$-table, we have

$$
Φ(0.67)=0.7486.
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(16\le Y\le 20)=2Φ(0.67)-1=0.4972.
$$"] ["question-4bd1cff1-6c69-5338-8c54-dfce19778dbc" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-effd6099-f4df-5d9b-a019-343ae34a858c" :answer-field/id #uuid I.I.D random variables, where

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(-0.05,{0.1}^{2}),\,1\le i\le 100,
$$

calculate $P(Y\ge -4.25),$ where  $Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{100}.$

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ |

| $\,0.7\,$ | $\,0.7642\,$ | $\,0.7673\,$ | $\,0.7704\,$ | $\,0.7734\,$ |
| $\,0.8\,$ | $\,0.7939\,$ | $\,0.7967\,$ | $\,0.7995\,$ | $\,0.8023\,$ |"] ["question-cd6eb665-f20f-5952-b033-241935d01495" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed (I.I.D) normal random variables, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then 

$$
Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{n}∼N(n\mu ,\,n{\sigma }^{2}).
$$

Therefore, since ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{100}$ are independent and identically distributed, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{100} & ∼N(100\cdot (-0.05),\,100\cdot {0.1}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(100\cdot (-0.05),\,100\cdot 0.01) \\  & =N(-5,1).\end{aligned}
$$

We wish to compute the probability $P(Y\ge -4.25).$ We first convert $Y$ into a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\ge -4.25) & =P(Z\ge \frac{-4.25-(-5)}{\sqrt{1}}) \\  & =P(Z\ge 0.75) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 0.75) \\  & =1-Φ(0.75)\end{aligned}
$$

From the $z$-table, we have

$$
Φ(0.75)=0.7734.
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(Y\ge -4.25)=1-Φ(0.75)=0.2266.
$$"] ["question-cd6eb665-f20f-5952-b033-241935d01495" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-1a7cc0cb-6474-5b58-baaf-724c624eae6f" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-227f2a32-4a18-5560-9e21-65c9391f9977" :question/math-academy-id "q-152018"] ["question-227f2a32-4a18-5560-9e21-65c9391f9977" :question/problem "A sports shop sells table tennis balls in boxes of $6.$ The weight of a table tennis ball, in grams, is normally distributed with a mean of $2.72\,\text{g}$ and a standard deviation of $0.05\,\text{g},$ while the weight of a box, in grams, is normally distributed with a mean of $12\,\text{g}$ and a standard deviation of $2\,\text{g}.$ If one box full of balls is randomly selected, what is the probability that it weighs less than $30\,\text{g}?$
You may assume that the weights are mutually independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*

| $z$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.7\,$ | $\,0.7611\,$ | $\,0.7642\,$ | $\,0.7673\,$ | $\,0.7704\,$ |
| $\,0.8\,$ | $\,0.7910\,$ | $\,0.7939\,$ | $\,0.7967\,$ | $\,0.7995\,$ |
| $\,0.9\,$ | $\,0.8186\,$ | $\,0.8212\,$ | $\,0.8238\,$ | $\,0.8264\,$ |"] ["question-227f2a32-4a18-5560-9e21-65c9391f9977" :question/worked-solution "Let ${X}_{i}$ denote the weight of the $i$th ball, and let $Y$ denote the weight of a box. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(2.72,{0.05}^{2}),\,1\le i\le 6,
$$

and

$$
Y∼N(12,{2}^{2}).
$$

Let the random variable $W$ denote the weight of a randomly selected box of balls. Then, since

$$
W={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{6}+Y,
$$

we have that $W$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[W] & =6\cdot 2.72+12 \\  & =28.32 \\ \text{Var}[W] & =6\cdot {0.05}^{2}+{2}^{2} \\  & =4.015.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
W∼N(28.32,4.015).
$$

In order to find $P(W<30),$ we convert $W$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(W<30) & =P(Z<\frac{30-28.32}{\sqrt{4.015}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<0.84) \\  & =Φ(0.84)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(0.84)≈0.7995.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(W<30) & ≈Φ(0.84) \\  & ≈0.7995.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-227f2a32-4a18-5560-9e21-65c9391f9977" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-df5b89bb-72ac-5d01-aa77-b021461d13e3" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-227f2a32-4a18-5560-9e21-65c9391f9977"] [17592186188562 :question/problem "A math test is composed of $15$ exercises. The time that a student takes to solve an exercise, in minutes, is normally distributed with a mean of $6\,\text{min}$ and a standard deviation of $2\,\text{min}.$ If one student is randomly selected, what is the probability that they will take between $80\,\text{min}$ and $100\,\text{min}$ to complete all exercises? You may assume that the times spent solving each exercise are mutually independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ | $\,0.09\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,1.0\,$ | $\,0.8554\,$ | $\,0.8577\,$ | $\,0.8599\,$ | $\,0.8621\,$ |
| $\,1.1\,$ | $\,0.8770\,$ | $\,0.8790\,$ | $\,0.8810\,$ | $\,0.8830\,$ |
| $\,1.2\,$ | $\,0.8962\,$ | $\,0.8980\,$ | $\,0.8997\,$ | $\,0.9015\,$ |"] [17592186188562 :question/worked-solution "Let ${X}_{i}$ denote the time spent solving the $i$th exercise. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(60,{2}^{2}),\,1\le i\le 15.
$$

Let the random variable $W$ denote the time it takes a randomly selected student to complete the test. Then, since

$$
W={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{15},
$$

we have that $W$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[W] & =15\cdot 6 \\  & =90, \\ \text{Var}[W] & =15\cdot {2}^{2} \\  & =60.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
W∼N(90,60).
$$

In order to find $P(80<W<100),$ we convert $W$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(80<W<100) & =P(\frac{80-90}{\sqrt{60}}<Z<\frac{100-90}{\sqrt{60}}) \\  & ≈P(-1.29<Z<1.29) \\  & =Φ(1.29)-Φ(-1.29) \\  & =Φ(1.29)-(1-Φ(1.29)) \\  & =2Φ(1.29)-1\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(1.29)≈0.9015.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(80<W<100) & ≈2Φ(1.29)-1 \\  & ≈0.8030.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186188562 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] [17592186185652 :answer-field/correct 17592186185656] ["question-77a63100-6b22-5680-ab48-c534778dd5f2" :question/id #uuid "77a63100-6b22-5680-ab48-c534778dd5f2"] ["question-77a63100-6b22-5680-ab48-c534778dd5f2" :question/math-academy-id "q-143391"] ["question-77a63100-6b22-5680-ab48-c534778dd5f2" :question/problem "A bouquet consists of $20$ roses. *Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $\,1.4\,$ | $\,0.9251\,$ | $\,0.9265\,$ | $\,0.9279\,$ | $\,0.9292\,$ |"] ["question-77a63100-6b22-5680-ab48-c534778dd5f2" :question/worked-solution "Let ${X}_{i}$ denote the weight of the $i$th rose. Then, we have

$$

$$

Let the random variable $W$ denote the weight of a randomly selected bouquet. Then, since

$$
W={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{20},
$$

we have that $W$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[W] & =20\cdot 70 \\  & =1\,400, \\ \text{Var}[W] & =20\cdot {5}^{2} \\  & =500.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
W∼N(1\,400,500).
$$

In order to find $P(W>1\,430),$ we convert $W$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(W>1\,430) & =P(Z>\frac{1\,430-1\,400}{\sqrt{500}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>1.34) \\  & =1-P(Z<1.34) \\  & =1-Φ(1.34)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(1.34)≈0.9099.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(W>1\,430) & ≈1-Φ(1.34) \\  & ≈0.0901.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-77a63100-6b22-5680-ab48-c534778dd5f2" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-bbc26b25-958d-58de-aac7-dce04e49cb32" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-9f941d6e-0531-597c-97c5-4e948faf202b" :question/math-academy-id "q-110258"] ["question-9f941d6e-0531-597c-97c5-4e948faf202b" :question/problem "In a certain shop, eggs are sold in cartons by the dozen.
The weight of an egg, in grams, is normally distributed with a mean of $65\,\text{g}$ and a standard deviation of $5\,\text{g},$ while the weight of an egg carton, in grams, is normally distributed with a mean of $50\,\text{g}$ and a standard deviation of $2\,\text{g}.$
If one carton filled with eggs is randomly selected, what is the probability that it weighs more than $850\,\text{g}?$ You may assume that the weights are independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,1.0\,$ | $\,0.8461\,$ | $\,0.8485\,$ | $\,0.8508\,$ | $\,0.8531\,$ |
| $\,1.1\,$ | $\,0.8686\,$ | $\,0.8708\,$ | $\,0.8729\,$ | $\,0.8749\,$ |
| $\,1.2\,$ | $\,0.8888\,$ | $\,0.8907\,$ | $\,0.8925\,$ | $\,0.8944\,$ |"] ["question-9f941d6e-0531-597c-97c5-4e948faf202b" :question/worked-solution "Let ${X}_{i}$ denote the weight of the $i$th egg, and let $Y$ denote the weight of a carton. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(65,{5}^{2}),\,1\le i\le 12,
$$

and

$$
Y∼N(50,{2}^{2}).
$$

Let the random variable $W$ denote the weight of a randomly selected carton filled with eggs. Then, since

$$
W={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{12}+Y,
$$

we have that $W$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[W] & =12\cdot 65+50 \\  & =830, \\ \text{Var}[W] & =12\cdot {5}^{2}+{2}^{2} \\  & =304.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
W∼N(830,304).
$$

In order to find $P(W>850),$ we convert $W$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(W>850) & =P(Z>\frac{850-830}{\sqrt{304}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>1.15) \\  & =1-P(Z<1.15) \\  & =1-Φ(1.15)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(1.15)≈0.8749.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(W>850) & ≈1-Φ(1.15) \\  & ≈1-0.8749 \\  & =0.1251.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-9f941d6e-0531-597c-97c5-4e948faf202b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-1e990cf7-ee17-56d4-bac7-fe509d55e818" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$"] [17592186221931 :question/worked-solution "Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$

where 

$$
s-2>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+2.
$$"] [17592186304980 :question/problem "Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the Laplace transform is $L\{f(t)\}=F(s).$ How can we obtain the graph of $L\{{e}^{8t}f(t)\}$ from the graph of $F(s)?$"] [17592186304980 :question/worked-solution "The first shifting theorem states that if

$L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$
then
$L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by ${e}^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a>0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a<0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of $L\{{e}^{t}f(t)\},$ we must shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $1$ unit to the right.

:question/problem "Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=6t+4{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}$ for $s>2.$"] ["question-8828e2f6-2765-54b6-be68-2960b77fe33e" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{6t+4{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =L\{6t\}+L\{4{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =6L\{t\}+4L\{{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t\} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}} \\ L\{{t}^{3}\} & =\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
L\{{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}\}=\frac{6}{(s-2)^{4}}.
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =6L\{t\}+4L\{{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =6\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+4\cdot \frac{6}{(s-2)^{4}} \\  & =\frac{6}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{24}{(s-2)^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>2.$"] ["question-8828e2f6-2765-54b6-be68-2960b77fe33e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-d796c28f-05c4-5d13-97d9-d47a85425db2" ["question-48f6d6fb-eebd-57a1-90a2-1f718d690dc4" :question/math-academy-id "q-68813"] ["question-48f6d6fb-eebd-57a1-90a2-1f718d690dc4" :question/problem "Jane is making lemonade for her friends. According to the recipe, $4$ cups of lemon juice are required for $18$ glasses of lemonade. There is a proportional relationship between the number of cups of lemon juice and the number of glasses of lemonade. If Jane needs to make $12$ glasses of lemonade, how many cups of lemon juice does she need?"] ["question-48f6d6fb-eebd-57a1-90a2-1f718d690dc4" :question/worked-solution "Let $x$ be the number of cups of lemon juice and $y$ be the number of glasses of lemonade.

First, we need to construct the equation that represents the proportional relationship. Every proportional relationship takes the form $y=kx,$ where $k$ is the constant of proportionality.

We are told that $x=4$ cups of lemon juice are required for $y=18$ glasses of lemonade. We can find the constant of proportionality by computing the ratio of the $y$-value to the $x$-value, as follows:

$$
k=\frac{y}{x}=\frac{18}{4}=\frac{18÷2}{4÷2}=\frac{9}{2}
$$

Therefore, the equation is

$$
y=\frac{9}{2}x.
$$

Now, we want to find the value of $x$ so that Jane can make $y=12$ glasses of lemonade. So, we substitute $y=12$ into the equation above:

$$
\begin{aligned}12 & =\frac{9}{2}x \\ \frac{9}{2}x & =12\end{aligned}
$$

To solve for $x,$ we multiply both sides of the equation by the reciprocal of $\frac{9}{2},$ which is $\frac{2}{9}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{9}\times \frac{9}{2}x & =\frac{2}{9}\times 12 \\ x & =\frac{2\times 12}{9} \\ x & =\frac{24}{9} \\ x & =\frac{24÷3}{9÷3} \\ x & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the resulting improper fraction as a mixed number:

$$
\frac{8}{3}=2\,\text{R}2=2\,\frac{2}{3}
$$

Therefore, Jane requires $2\,\frac{2}{3}$ cups of lemon juice to make $12$ glasses of lemonade."] ["question-48f6d6fb-eebd-57a1-90a2-1f718d690dc4" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] {{field-1}}"] ["question-3fee2173-5ead-559d-b784-c9f6f5226ecd" :question/worked-solution "Since $p$ varies directly with $q,$ we use the equation

$$
p=kq.
$$

We are told that $p=-35$ when $q=-7.$ We substitute this data into the equation to find $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-35 & =k\cdot (-7) \\ \frac{(-35)}{(-7)} & =k \\ \frac{35}{7} & =k \\ 5 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the direct variation equation is given by

$$
p=5q.
$$

Finally, substituting the value of $q=-6$ into this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =5\cdot (-6)=-30.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-3fee2173-5ead-559d-b784-c9f6f5226ecd" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-e95dfe78-b1e7-5a61-bce1-8aaf37b7c796" :answer-field/id #uuid "e95dfe78-b1e7-5a61-bce1-8aaf37b7c796"] ["answer-281ab47b-8c5b-5f64-bf9a-faea1728fdb6" :answer/id #uuid "281ab47b-8c5b-5f64-bf9a-faea1728fdb6"] ["answer-281ab47b-8c5b-5f64-bf9a-faea1728fdb6" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-281ab47b-8c5b-5f64-bf9a-faea1728fdb6" :answer/value "-30"] ["answer-field-e95dfe78-b1e7-5a61-bce1-8aaf37b7c796" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-e95dfe78-b1e7-5a61-bce1-8aaf37b7c796" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-e95dfe78-b1e7-5a61-bce1-8aaf37b7c796" :answer-field/correct "answer-281ab47b-8c5b-5f64-bf9a-faea1728fdb6"] ["answer-field-e95dfe78-b1e7-5a61-bce1-8aaf37b7c796" :answer-field/choices "answer-281ab47b-8c5b-5f64-bf9a-faea1728fdb6"] ["question-3fee2173-5ead-559d-b784-c9f6f5226ecd" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-e95dfe78-b1e7-5a61-bce1-8aaf37b7c796"] [17592186152272 :knowledge-point/questions "question-3fee2173-5ead-559d-b784-c9f6f5226ecd"] [17592186153437 :tutorial/content "Recall that two variables, $x$ and $y,$ are said to have a proportional relationship if their ratio is constant. Let's see an example."] [17592186152312 :activity/expected-seconds 480.0] ["question-e1b5df81-7853-5e90-b2a0-96b74729c9c8" :question/id #uuid "e1b5df81-7853-5e90-b2a0-96b74729c9c8"] ["question-e1b5df81-7853-5e90-b2a0-96b74729c9c8" :question/math-academy-id "q-79749"] ["question-e1b5df81-7853-5e90-b2a0-96b74729c9c8" :question/problem "Given a right triangular prism, find the differential $\text{d}V$ for the volume $V$ if the height is $h=1$ and the base is a right triangle with legs $a=2$ and $b=4.$"] ["question-e1b5df81-7853-5e90-b2a0-96b74729c9c8" :question/worked-solution "The volume of a given right triangular prism is $V=\frac{abh}{2}.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(a,b,c) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂V}{∂b})\,\text{d}b+(\frac{∂V}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =\frac{bh}{2}\,\text{d}a+\frac{ah}{2}\,\text{d}b+\frac{ab}{2}\,\text{d}h\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=2,$ $b=4,$ and $h=1,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(2,4,1) & =\frac{4\cdot 1}{2}\,\text{d}a+\frac{2\cdot 1}{2}\,\text{d}b+\frac{2\cdot 4}{2}\,\text{d}h \\  & =2\,\text{d}a+\text{d}b+4\,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-e1b5df81-7853-5e90-b2a0-96b74729c9c8" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-361b4f31-81d9-5f43-b63b-1aa713ee6c5a" :answer-field/id #uuid </tr></tbody></table>"] [17592186365659 :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & -6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=6\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-6\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((6\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(6\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(6\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+6\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot \frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}].
$$"] ["answer-4148c3f6-7cd3-5b8a-8b0b-2b61c22f4d78" :answer/id #uuid "4148c3f6-7cd3-5b8a-8b0b-2b61c22f4d78"] ["answer-4148c3f6-7cd3-5b8a-8b0b-2b61c22f4d78" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-4148c3f6-7cd3-5b8a-8b0b-2b61c22f4d78" :answer/value "\cos(6t)"] [17592186365662 :answer-field/correct "answer-4148c3f6-7cd3-5b8a-8b0b-2b61c22f4d78"] [17592186365662 :answer-field/choices "answer-4148c3f6-7cd3-5b8a-8b0b-2b61c22f4d78"] ["answer-0d0d2d29-ff61-5f5f-b6b0-49c8e2ecf0ba" :answer/id #uuid "0d0d2d29-ff61-5f5f-b6b0-49c8e2ecf0ba"] ["answer-0d0d2d29-ff61-5f5f-b6b0-49c8e2ecf0ba" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-0d0d2d29-ff61-5f5f-b6b0-49c8e2ecf0ba" :answer/value "-\sin(6t)"] [17592186365664 :answer-field/correct "answer-0d0d2d29-ff61-5f5f-b6b0-49c8e2ecf0ba"] [17592186365664 :answer-field/choices "answer-0d0d2d29-ff61-5f5f-b6b0-49c8e2ecf0ba"] ["answer-06aa85f1-3426-574e-99c1-322400e91930" :answer/id #uuid "06aa85f1-3426-574e-99c1-322400e91930"] ["answer-06aa85f1-3426-574e-99c1-322400e91930" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-06aa85f1-3426-574e-99c1-322400e91930" :answer/value "\sin(6t)"] [17592186365660 :answer-field/correct "answer-06aa85f1-3426-574e-99c1-322400e91930"] [17592186365660 :answer-field/choices "answer-06aa85f1-3426-574e-99c1-322400e91930"] ["answer-873e1c15-5d9d-58fe-a62d-ab1be804a1ea" :answer/id #uuid "873e1c15-5d9d-58fe-a62d-ab1be804a1ea"] ["answer-873e1c15-5d9d-58fe-a62d-ab1be804a1ea" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-873e1c15-5d9d-58fe-a62d-ab1be804a1ea" :answer/value "\cos(6t)"] [17592186365666 :answer-field/correct "answer-873e1c15-5d9d-58fe-a62d-ab1be804a1ea"] [17592186365666 :answer-field/choices "answer-873e1c15-5d9d-58fe-a62d-ab1be804a1ea"] ["question-3f77715c-0903-5f4b-a449-6816c6d9bb06" :question/id #uuid "3f77715c-0903-5f4b-a449-6816c6d9bb06"] ["question-3f77715c-0903-5f4b-a449-6816c6d9bb06" :question/math-academy-id "q-334465"] ["question-3f77715c-0903-5f4b-a449-6816c6d9bb06" :question/problem "$$

The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ 0 & 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=4t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=7t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(4t)={e}^{4t} \\ r(7t)={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{4t} \\ 7t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{4t} \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{7t}\end{aligned}].

$A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for all $t$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the {{field-1}} of {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-3}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line {{field-4}} by the properties of invertible matrices."] ["question-3fdf52f0-09f2-54b2-864b-627c885837ad" :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first interpret line $\text{L1}.$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the $\text{columns}$ of $Φ,$ namely the functions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$ These functions are the fundamental solutions of the system.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Recall that a square matrix is invertible when its determinant is nonzero. Since in $\text{L3}$ we have that $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t,$ it follows that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t.$ Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by the properties of invertible matrices."] ["question-d656b9e3-27c9-51a6-a70f-c9d56643be83" :question/problem "Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-3}} by the transitive property of equality."] ["question-d656b9e3-27c9-51a6-a70f-c9d56643be83" :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ In $\text{L3}$ we have $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t),$ and in $\text{L4}$ we have $Φ(t)c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).$ For example, the line $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{EF}$ in the diagram below is a transversal.

![](images/cd/cdae3e21ca7b66c756e047b2f71dd03d1320a947e7477f6b025dacef95321399.png)

A pair of parallel lines with a transversal form a set of $8$ angles, shown below.

![](images/a4/a4465bbe051f978925e704cc40ced894c4e8c6625c53c7bd944a93c123359ab9.png)

This set of eight angles can be grouped into two categories:

- We have four pairs of **vertical angles**:

![](images/e0/e010db0c586e29e8ae640842f1519da314455bb7520680b80530799509058df3.png)

- We also have four pairs of so-called **corresponding angles**:

![](images/d1/d1b3f1ede08e3c20c80b7a23477491237e73a9b6691d93e6deabc5e5a4e0c57b.png)

Corresponding pairs of angles are located in the same position as each other relative to the parallel lines and on the same side of the transversal. Pairs of corresponding angles are congruent."] [17592186070008 :tutorial/content "Consider the following pair of parallel lines $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{AB} \parallel \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{CD},$ and the transversal $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{EF}.$

![](images/af/af403ef4827e840a49d5a3bde36561d22a508d262b3ad15b830812aefc306286.png)

 What is the value of $x?$

First, note that $\angle DIF$ and $\angle BJI$ are corresponding angles. Therefore, they are congruent and thus have the same measure. This means we can write down the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠DIF & =m∠BJI \\ 3x-{20}^{∘} & =x+{10}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this equation, we first subtract $x$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-{20}^{∘} & =x+{10}^{∘} \\ 3x-{20}^{∘}-x & =x+{10}^{∘}-x \\ 2x-{20}^{∘} & ={10}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we add $20^\circ$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-{20}^{∘} & ={10}^{∘} \\ 2x-{20}^{∘}+{20}^{∘} & ={10}^{∘}+{20}^{∘} \\ 2x & ={30}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides by $2{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & ={30}^{∘} \\ \frac{2x}{2} & =\frac{{30}^{∘}}{2} \\ \frac{\cancel{2}x}{\cancel{2}} & ={15}^{∘} \\ x & ={15}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=15^\circ.$"] [17592186068954 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] ["question-3039fef2-75f2-578d-b446-f0e62f788f69" :question/id #uuid "3039fef2-75f2-578d-b446-f0e62f788f69"] ["question-3039fef2-75f2-578d-b446-f0e62f788f69" :question/math-academy-id "q-143270"] ["question-3039fef2-75f2-578d-b446-f0e62f788f69" :question/problem "Given that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{25}∼N(-6,{15}^{2})$ is a random sample of size $n=25$ from a normal population, what is the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}?$"] ["question-3039fef2-75f2-578d-b446-f0e62f788f69" :question/worked-solution "If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$

$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
n=25,\,\mu =-6,\,\sigma =15.
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(-6,\frac{{15}^{2}}{25}) \\  & ∼N(-6,9).\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-3039fef2-75f2-578d-b446-f0e62f788f69" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-493b3d3c-49a6-53e5-bb2a-8fbde7a2ceee" :answer-field/id #uuid | $\,0.3\,$ | $\,0.6179\,$ | $\,0.6217\,$ | $\,0.6255\,$ | $\,0.6293\,$ | $\,0.6331\,$ | $\,0.6368\,$ |"] ["question-e261753e-ab38-5195-b690-27439e259444" :question/worked-solution "If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(7,\frac{{14}^{2}}{49}) \\  & ∼N(7,4).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7.5).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7.5) & =P(\frac{6.8-7}{\sqrt{4}}<Z<\frac{7.5-7}{\sqrt{4}}) \\  & =P(-0.1<Z<0.25) \\  & =Φ(0.25)-Φ(-0.1)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.25)=0.5987,\end{aligned}
$$

and by the symmetry of the normal distribution,

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.1) & =1-Φ(0.1) \\  & =1-0.5398 \\  & =0.4602.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7.5) & =Φ(0.25)-Φ(-0.1) \\  & =0.5987-0.4602 \\  & =0.1385.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-e261753e-ab38-5195-b690-27439e259444" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-a6304b95-a451-5219-83db-3e96f7493cf2" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

 then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

We're told that the population mean $\mu =15,$ the population standard deviation $\sigma =2,$ and that the sample size $n=16.$ Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(15,\frac{{2}^{2}}{16}) \\  & ∼N(15,0.25).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(14.7<\overset{―}{X}<15.3).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(14.7<\overset{―}{X}<15.3) & =P(\frac{14.7-15}{\sqrt{0.25}}<Z<\frac{15.3-15}{\sqrt{0.25}}) \\  & =P(-0.6<Z<0.6) \\  & =Φ(0.6)-Φ(-0.6)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.6) & ≈0.7257 \\ Φ(-0.6) & ≈0.2743.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(14.7<\overset{―}{X}<15.3) & =Φ(0.6)-Φ(-0.6) \\  & ≈0.7257-0.2743 \\  & =0.4514.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-18e0dc2d-9409-5746-a133-14c7fa279d0a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-2fa5dcaf-135b-527a-9eda-ec86e48eb63a" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "If $y$ varies inversely with $x$ and $y=10$ when $x=\frac{3}{2},$ find the value of $y$ when $x=3.$"] ["question-19618a93-f5c7-57b8-b5e4-4ba96b1ca9c7" :question/worked-solution "Since $y$ varies inversely with $x,$ we use the equation

$$
y=\frac{k}{x}.
$$

We are told that $y=10$ when $x=\frac{3}{2}.$ We substitute this data into the equation to find $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =\frac{k}{(\frac{3}{2})} \\ 10\cdot (\frac{3}{2}) & =k \\ \frac{30}{2} & =k \\ 15 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the inverse variation is given by 

$$
y=\frac{15}{x}.
$$

Finally, substituting the value of $x=3$ into this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{15}{3}=5.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-19618a93-f5c7-57b8-b5e4-4ba96b1ca9c7" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-7738aed2-6969-583c-b1d2-159e3752029b" :answer-field/id #uuid The more water that we add, the less that we'll be able to taste the orange. 

More precisely, the concentration of pure orange $y$ (in grams per liter) varies **inversely** with the volume $x$ (in liters) of water added. We can express this idea using an **inverse variation equation** as follows:

$$
y= \dfrac{k}{x}
$$

The constant $k$ is called the **constant of variation** or **constant of proportionality.**

Notice that:

- If $x$ is small (i.e., there is not much water), then $y$ is large (i.e., there is a high concentration of orange).

- If $x$ is large (i.e., there is lots of water), then $y$ is small (i.e., there is a low concentration of orange).

To find the constant of variation $k$, we need to plug in some data. 

For example, suppose we know that the concentration is $y = 200\, \textrm{g/L}$ when $x = 4\,\textrm L$ of water has been added. Plugging this into our relationship and solving for $k,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{k}{x} \\ 200 & =\frac{k}{4} \\ 200\cdot 4 & =k \\ 800 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the relationship between $y$ and $x$ is

$$
y = \dfrac {800} x.
$$

Finally, notice that we can rewrite the above relationship as

$$
xy = 800.
$$"] [17592186139720 :tutorial/content "If  $y$ varies inversely with  $x,$ then we can also say that $y$ is **inversely proportional** to $x.$ We can express this mathematically as

$$
y \propto \dfrac{1}{x},
$$

where $\propto$ is the proportionality symbol.

The following statements are equivalent:

- $y = \dfrac{k}{x}$ for some constant $k$

- $y$ varies inversely with $x$

- $y$ is inversely proportional to $x$

- $y \propto \dfrac{1}{x}$"] [17592186138599 :activity/expected-seconds 720.0]] "retractions" [[17592186228929 :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $90\cos(6t)\,\textrm{V},$ a resistor with resistance $30\,\Omega,$ and a capacitor with capacitance $\dfrac1{150}\,\textrm{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I = \dfrac{\textrm d q}{\textrm d t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R = 30\,\Omega.$ So,

$$
V_R = 30I = 30\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore,

$$
V_C = \dfrac{q}{\left(\dfrac1{150}\right)} = 150q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
90\cos(6t) = 30\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 150q,
$$

which gives

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 5q = 3\cos(6t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution $q_c,$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q_c}{\mathrm{d}t} + 5q_c = 0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
q_c(t) = Ae^{-5t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $6t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $6t,$ i.e.,

$$
q_p(t) = \alpha\cos(6t) + \beta\sin(6t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-6\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+6\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-6\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+6\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t))+5(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ (-6\alpha +5\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+(5\alpha +6\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-6\alpha +5\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)) \\ 5\alpha +6\beta =3\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha = \dfrac{15}{61}, \beta = \dfrac{18}{61}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
q_p(t) = \dfrac{15}{61}\cos(6t) + \dfrac{18}{61}\sin(6t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t) = q_c(t) + q_p(t) = Ae^{-5t} + \dfrac{15}{61}\cos(6t) + \dfrac{18}{61}\sin(6t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity $q_c(t) = Ae^{-5t}$ is the *transient charge*, since it goes to zero as $t \to \infty.$

- The function $q_p(t) = \dfrac{15}{61}\cos(6t) + \dfrac{18}{61}\sin(6t)$ is the *steady-state charge*. It governs the charge's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to\infty,$ we have

$$
q(t)\approx q_p(t) = \dfrac{15}{61}\cos(6t) + \dfrac{18}{61}\sin(6t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state charge, in coulombs, is given by

$$
\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{15}{61}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{18}{61}\right)^2} \approx 0.38,
$$

rounded to two decimal places."] [17592186229691 :question/problem "![](images/72/726e1c886236a47159bf154fc1ad6384ffc4aa89c5b3cba6b0067a70a0a773f2.png)

$$

$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore,

Therefore, the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is also normally distributed, where

$$
\overline{X}\sim N\left(\mu,\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)
$$

By transforming $\overline{X}$ to a standard normal random variable, we have

$$
Z = \dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\sim N(0,1)
$$

We wish to find a $z$-interval that we're $95\%$ confident that the random variable $Z$ lies within. This interval is indicated in the diagram below:

![](images/50/50a0f49fe5c96ba3259832fbf1a0abcedffb342301ca069bb7b88d157a181019.png)

To help with the notation, we define a new parameter $\alpha$. Since we're computing a $95\%$ confidence interval, we have

$$
\alpha=1-0.95=0.05\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.025
$$

Notice that

$$
\dfrac{\alpha}{2}
$$

is precisely the area bounded by each "tail" that we're excluding from our confidence interval. Let's label the critical values at the endpoints of our interval as $\pm z_{\alpha/2}$:

![](images/3c/3cdfd2c72bf7fe65e5d1b584d46d4c846e74615e54c739a6d1ea990c95011a8a.png)

According to our diagram,

$$
P(Z > z_{0.025}) = P(Z < -z_{0.025}) = 0.025
$$

Using a percentage points table for the standard normal distribution, we find that

$$
z_{0.025} \approx 1.96
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(Z > 1.96) = P(Z < -1.96) = 0.025
$$

In other words,

$$
P(-1.96 < Z < 1.96) = 0.95
$$

Therefore, there is a $95\%$ probability that our random variable $Z$ will lie in the interval $(-1.96, 1.96)$.

Now, here's the trick. We solve the inequality inside the parentheses of the last probability statement for the population mean $\mu$:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-1.96 < & Z < 1.96 \\ -1.96 < & (x^(―) - μ)/(σ/\sqrt{n}) < 1.96 \\ -1.96 \cdot \frac{σ}{\sqrt{n}} < & x^(―) - μ < 1.96 \cdot \frac{σ}{\sqrt{n}} \\ -x^(―) - 1.96 \cdot \frac{σ}{\sqrt{n}} < & - μ < - x^(―) + 1.96 \cdot \frac{σ}{\sqrt{n}} \\ x^(―) + 1.96 \cdot \frac{σ}{\sqrt{n}} > & μ > x^(―) - 1.96 \cdot \frac{σ}{\sqrt{n}} \\ x^(―) - 1.96 \cdot \frac{σ}{\sqrt{n}} < & μ < x^(―) + 1.96 \cdot \frac{σ}{\sqrt{n}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Therefore, a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu$ is given by

$$
\left(\overline{x} - 1.96\cdot\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}},\: \overline{x} + 1.96\cdot\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)
$$

Finally, substituting our values

$$
n=10, \qquad \overline{x}=12, \qquad \sigma=3
$$

we obtain that our $95\%$ confidence interval for $\mu$ is

$$
\big(12- 1.859, \: 12 + 1.859 \big)
$$

Then, for a given value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1$, a $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu$ is given by

$$
\left(\overline{x} - z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}, \: \overline{x} + z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)
$$

where

$$
P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}
$$

and $Z \sim N(0,1)$.

The endpoints of our confidence interval are called **confidence limits** and are given by

$$
\overline{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
$$

Each part of the formula above has a name:

- $\overline{x}$ is an estimate of the population mean

More precisely, we have the following theorem:

> *If $X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n$ are mutually independent normal random variables such that*
> $X_1 \sim N(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2), \qquad X_2\sim (\mu_2,\sigma_2^2), \qquad \ldots, \quad X_n\sim(\mu_n,\sigma_n^2)$,
> *then the random variable*
> $Y=X_1+X_2+\ldots+X_n$
> *is normally distributed, where*
> $Y\sim N(\mu_1+\mu_2+\ldots+\mu_n, \: \sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2+\ldots+\sigma_n^2)$.

For example, if the random variables

$$
X_1\sim N({\color{blue}2},{\color{red}3}), \qquad X_2\sim N({\color{blue}1},{\color{red}4}), \qquad X_3\sim N({\color{blue}1},{\color{red}1})
$$

are mutually independent, then

$$
Y=X_1+X_2+X_3
$$

is normally distributed.

Let's figure out the distribution of $Y$. We start by computing its mean and variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[Y] &= μ_{1} + μ_{2} + μ_{3} \\
&= 2 + 1 + 1 \\
&= 4, \\
Var[Y] &= σ_{1}^{2} + σ_{2}^{2} + σ_{3}^{2} \\
&= 3 + 4 + 1 \\
&= 8
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
Y = X_{1} + X_{2} + X_{3} \mid ∼N(4, 8)
$$

**Watch out!** It is vital that $X_1, X_2,\ldots X_n$ are *mutually independent*."] [17592186177005 :tutorial/content "When we form a random variable $Y$ from a linear combination of mutually independent, normally distributed random variables, the distribution of $Y$ is also normal.

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$

{{field-1}}"] [17592186139718 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we're making a juice drink with a fixed amount of pure orange and the rest water.

The more water that we add, the less that we'll be able to taste the orange.

More precisely, the concentration of pure orange $y$ (in grams per liter) varies **inversely** with the volume $x$ (in liters) of water added. We can express this idea using an **inverse variation equation** as follows:

$$
y= \dfrac{k}{x}
$$

The constant $k$ is called the **constant of variation** or **constant of proportionality.**

Notice that:

- If $x$ is small (i.e., there is not much water), then $y$ is large (i.e., there is a high concentration of orange).
- If $x$ is large (i.e., there is lots of water), then $y$ is small (i.e., there is a low concentration of orange).

To find the constant of variation $k$, we need to plug in some data.

For example, suppose we know that the concentration is

$$
y = 200\, \textrm{g/L}
$$

when

$$
x = 4\,\textrm L
$$

of water has been added. Plugging this into our relationship and solving for $k$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= \frac{k}{x} \\
200 &= \frac{k}{4} \\
200 \cdot 4 &= k \\
800 &= k
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the relationship between $y$ and $x$ is

$$
y = \dfrac {800} x
$$

Finally, notice that we can rewrite the above relationship as

$$
xy = 800
$$"] [17592186139720 :tutorial/content "If $y$ varies inversely with $x$, then we can also say that $y$ is **inversely proportional** to $x$. We can express this mathematically as

$$
y \propto \dfrac{1}{x}
$$

where $\propto$ is the proportionality symbol.

The following statements are equivalent:

- $y = \dfrac{k}{x}$ for some constant $k$
- $y$ varies inversely with $x$
- $y$ is inversely proportional to $x$
- $y \propto \dfrac{1}{x}$"]]}

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I = \dfrac{\textrm d q}{\textrm d t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R = 80\,\Omega.$ So,

$$
V_R = 80I = 80\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore,

$$
V_C = \dfrac{q}{0.0025} = 400q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
20\sin(3t) = 80\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 400q,
$$

which gives

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 5q = \dfrac{1}{4}\sin(3t).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186051040} {:db/id 17592186229689 :question/id #uuid "98078170-917a-59af-8498-c60a5c30f522" :question/math-academy-id "q-336217"} {:db/id 17592186229691 :question/id #uuid "273c8997-da69-595e-88fa-e96806d37c3a" :question/math-academy-id "q-336224" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186229134 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c51535d3-6b6a-5df3-a41f-9bad8e2edfbe" :knowledge-point/title "Constructing an Equation Governing the Charge in an RC Circuit"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "89bad66f-c7c3-5784-bfc7-56f1f2f8d401" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{dq}{dt} + 250q = 6\cos (5t)" :db/id 17592186228328} {:answer/id #uuid "d0c729c0-e5e7-5f23-bdeb-7f697b252fa9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{dq}{dt} + 10q = 6\cos (5t)" :db/id 17592186228329} {:answer/id #uuid "f7e6dc66-5867-5a8f-abef-b7d98f00a1e5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{dq}{dt} + \frac{1}{10}q = \frac{6}{25}\cos (5t)" :db/id 17592186228330} {:answer/id #uuid "ff714f07-0e55-5e88-ab57-6f5f6b173994" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{dq}{dt} + 250q = \frac{6}{25}\cos (5t)" :db/id 17592186228331} {:answer/id #uuid "596ac213-0811-5853-a6d8-87c46836aa72" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{dq}{dt} + 10q = \frac{6}{25}\cos (5t)" :db/id 17592186228332}] :answer-field/id #uuid "9218d20b-e123-5c36-b095-458ccd19a1b8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186228327}] :question/problem "![](images/72/726e1c886236a47159bf154fc1ad6384ffc4aa89c5b3cba6b0067a70a0a773f2.png)

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*" :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $15\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $250\,Ω,$ and a capacitor of capacitance $0.004\,\text{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I=\frac{\text{d}q}{\text{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=250\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=250I=250\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{0.004}=250q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
15=250\,\frac{dq}{dt}+250q,
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}+q=\frac{3}{50}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186311790 :question/id #uuid "7b502da6-93c9-578a-9438-7bf48a08ae11" :question/math-academy-id "q-337062"} {:db/id 17592186311791 :question/id #uuid *Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*" :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $18\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $60\,Ω,$ and a capacitor of capacitance $0.003\,\text{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I=\frac{\text{d}q}{\text{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=60\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=60I=60\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{0.003}=\frac{1000}{3}q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
18\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)=60\,\frac{dq}{dt}+\frac{1000}{3}q,
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}+\frac{50}{9}q=\frac{3}{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186229135 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186228928 :question/id #uuid "28fd19b3-762a-572e-9b52-27e17093ad93" :question/math-academy-id "e-21762"} :knowledge-point/id "![](images/42/424cb52325c95f03708ed9ae5fe1d41e7b0d1c8bb8878e1dd8dc002aef214481.png)

Find an equation for the charge $q$ (in coulombs) on the capacitor in the circuit given in the diagram above, expressing your answer in terms of time $t$ (in seconds) **only**, and given that the initial charge is $\dfrac{1}{50}\,\textrm{C}.$

*Hint: The voltage drop $V_C$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C,$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*" :question/worked-solution "The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I = \dfrac{\textrm d q}{\textrm d t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R = 80\,\Omega.$So,

$$
V_R = 80I = 80\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore,

$$
V_C = \dfrac{q}{0.00125} = 800q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
24 = 80\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 800q,
$$

which gives

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 10q = \dfrac3{10}.
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution $q_c,$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q_c}{\mathrm{d}t} + 10q_c = 0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
q_c(t) = Ae^{-10t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
q_p(t) = \alpha.
$$

To find the value of $\alpha,$ we substitute $q_p = \alpha$ and $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q_p}{\mathrm{d}t} = (\alpha)' = 0$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0 + 10\alpha = \dfrac3{10}
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  \alpha = \dfrac3{100}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is $q_p(t) = \dfrac3{100}.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t) = q_c(t) + q_p(t) = Ae^{-10t} + \dfrac3{100}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\dfrac{1}{50}\,\textrm{C}$ on the capacitor. So, we can apply the initial condition $q(0) = \dfrac{1}{50},$ and solve for $A{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}q(0) & =\frac{1}{50} \\ A{e}^{-10(0)}+\frac{3}{100} & =\frac{1}{50} \\ A & =-\frac{1}{100}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $q(t){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}q(t) & =-\frac{1}{100}{e}^{-10t}+\frac{3}{100} \\  & =\frac{1}{100}(3-{e}^{-10t})\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity $q_c = -\dfrac1{100}e^{-10t}$ is the *transient charge*, since it goes to zero as $t \to \infty.$

- The constant $q_p = \dfrac3{100}$ is the *steady-state charge*. As $t\to\infty,$ the charge $q$ approaches the value of the steady-state charge."} {:db/id 17592186049370} {:db/id 17592186049543} {:db/id 17592186229690 :question/id #uuid "1d398193-dedd-5f43-8339-eea51210db6e" :question/math-academy-id "q-336222"} {:db/id 17592186229695 :question/id #uuid "9547864c-5c79-5eab-ae35-a6351dc3262f" :question/math-academy-id "q-336594" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186229135 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1b88fec8-167e-5900-9ae8-109affedf08c" :knowledge-point/title "Solving an Equation Governing the Charge in an RC Circuit: Constant EMF"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2f6cd3ff-224c-593a-8d47-079eff9bf967" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{12}" :db/id 17592186309108}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "2f6cd3ff-224c-593a-8d47-079eff9bf967" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{12}" :db/id 17592186309108} :answer-field/id #uuid "542570a0-64d5-56eb-ab34-83a544b88a69" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186311009}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "The charge $q(t),$ in coulombs, in a series RC circuit is governed by the differential equation

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}+6q=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Find the steady-state charge for this circuit.

The steady-state charge is
{{field-1}} coulombs." :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "The given equation is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+6{q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-6t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha .
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${q}_{p}=\alpha $ and $\frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt}=(\alpha )^{′}=0$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0+6\alpha =\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\alpha =\frac{1}{12}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is ${q}_{p}(t)=\frac{1}{12}.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t)={q}_{c}(t)+{q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-6t}+\frac{1}{12}.
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${q}_{c}=A{e}^{-6t}$ is the *transient charge*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The constant ${q}_{p}=\frac{1}{12}$ is the *steady-state charge*. As $t\to \infty ,$ the charge $q$ approaches the value of the steady-state charge.

Therefore, the steady-state charge is $\frac{1}{12}$ coulombs."} {:db/id 17592186311723 :question/id #uuid "4200df25-ff4d-51eb-831b-f34b10d9d8a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-336590"} {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "A series RC circuit has a source electromotive force (EMF) of $24\,\text{V},$ a resistance of $75\,Ω,$ and a capacitance of $0.002\,\text{F}.$ Find, in coulombs rounded to three decimal places, the circuit capacitor's charge after $0.06$ seconds, given that the initial charge is $\frac{1}{40}$ coulombs.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*" :question/worked-solution "The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I=\frac{\text{d}q}{\text{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=75\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=75I=75\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{0.002}=500q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
24=75\,\frac{dq}{dt}+500q,
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}+\frac{20}{3}q=\frac{8}{25}.
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+\frac{20}{3}{q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-20t/3},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha .
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${q}_{p}=\alpha $ and $\frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt}=(\alpha )^{′}=0$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0+\frac{20}{3}\alpha =\frac{8}{25}\,⟹\,\alpha =\frac{6}{125}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is ${q}_{p}(t)=\frac{6}{125}.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t)={q}_{c}(t)+{q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-20t/3}+\frac{6}{125}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\frac{1}{40}\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor. So, we can apply the initial condition $q(0)=\frac{1}{40},$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}q(0) & =\frac{1}{40} \\ A{e}^{-20(0)/3}+\frac{6}{125} & =\frac{1}{40} \\ A & =-\frac{23}{1000}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $q(t):$

$$
q(t)=\frac{6}{125}-\frac{23}{1000}{e}^{-20t/3}
$$

Finally, the charge on the capacitor in the circuit after $t=0.06$ seconds, in coulombs, is

$$
q(0.06)=\frac{6}{125}-\frac{23}{1000}{e}^{-20(0.06)/3}≈0.033,
$$

rounded to three decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186229136 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186228929 :question/id #uuid "a3e7a060-f36d-5fd6-a6f6-5b321261fb0d" :question/math-academy-id "![](images/96/962694e1706c47a4b060da6636e0b6e2f1653cb94137dca8dc59781cf74bd252.png)

Find the amplitude of the steady-state charge for the RC circuit shown above, in coulombs, rounded to two decimal places. 

*Hint: The voltage drop $V_C$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C,$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*" :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $90\cos(6t)\,\textrm{V},$ a resistor with resistance $30\,\Omega,$ and a capacitor with capacitance $\dfrac1{150}\,\textrm{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I = \dfrac{\textrm d q}{\textrm d t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R = 30\,\Omega.$ So,

$$
V_R = 30I = 30\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore,

$$
V_C = \dfrac{q}{\left(\dfrac1{150}\right)} = 150q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
90\cos(6t) = 30\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 150q,
$$

which gives

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 5q = 3\cos(6t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution $q_c,$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q_c}{\mathrm{d}t} + 5q_c = 0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
q_c(t) = Ae^{-5t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $6t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $6t,$ i.e.,

$$
q_p(t) = \alpha\cos(6t) + \beta\sin(6t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-6\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+6\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-6\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+6\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t))+5(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ (-6\alpha +5\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+(5\alpha +6\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-6\alpha +5\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)) \\ 5\alpha +6\beta =3\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha = \dfrac{15}{61}, \beta = \dfrac{18}{61}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
q_p(t) = \dfrac{15}{61}\cos(6t) + \dfrac{18}{61}\sin(6t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t) = q_c(t) + q_p(t) = Ae^{-5t} + \dfrac{15}{61}\cos(6t) + \dfrac{18}{61}\sin(6t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity $q_c(t) = Ae^{-5t}$ is the *transient charge*, since it goes to zero as $t \to \infty.$

- The function $q_p(t) = \dfrac{15}{61}\cos(6t) + \dfrac{18}{61}\sin(6t)$ is the *steady-state charge*. It governs the charge's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to\infty,$ we have

$$
q(t)\approx q_p(t) = \dfrac{15}{61}\cos(6t) + \dfrac{18}{61}\sin(6t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state charge, in coulombs, is given by

$$
\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{15}{61}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{18}{61}\right)^2} \approx 0.38,
$$

rounded to two decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186048430} {:db/id 17592186049442} {:db/id 17592186050392} {:db/id 17592186229696 :question/id #uuid "f75fdde8-1a31-5115-9dda-a22cf62a4bb5" :question/math-academy-id "q-336636"} {:db/id 17592186229702 :question/id #uuid "d0d9a933-a0e8-56f2-b25b-1f97723df869" :question/math-academy-id "q-337169" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186229136 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "96b32f48-aea6-5ccd-94e9-47141767a803" :knowledge-point/title "Solving an Equation Governing the Charge in an RC Circuit: Sinusoidal EMF"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a68a0bc6-f30d-5411-b064-805f776486bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.4" :db/id 17592186228392} {:answer/id #uuid "bec5c4a2-e69a-58a3-94b3-3a681c2ec258" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.2" :db/id 17592186228393} {:answer/id #uuid "3f269fd6-b9ae-5b17-b3d5-9362d69d8e71" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.3" :db/id 17592186228394} {:answer/id #uuid "42cbcc13-0825-57af-be0a-c07b85f4c34d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.25" :db/id 17592186228395} {:answer/id #uuid "67173ceb-8d72-5892-b1ac-cf5cbde74ac5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.15" :db/id 17592186228396}] :answer-field/id #uuid "d8042cd1-bac2-5d2b-b9a4-591acf3abc28" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186228391}] :question/problem "![](images/a4/a4182416a97e5f0111b0823d6699f0ed39125f60289d7c7ebbb5f98d51d1a0f6.png)

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "![](images/f1/f1568a632a02f644f7ef8c39417bb06973f0862494aa0c3c624880a87c5620ee.png)

Find the amplitude of the steady-state charge for the RC circuit shown above, in coulombs, rounded to two decimal places. 

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*" :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $50\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor with resistance $25\,Ω,$ and a capacitor with capacitance $\frac{1}{100}\,\text{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I=\frac{\text{d}q}{\text{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=25\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=25I=25\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{(\frac{1}{100})}=100q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
50\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)=25\,\frac{dq}{dt}+100q,
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}+4q=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+4{q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-4t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $5t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $5t,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-5\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)+5\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-5\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)+5\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t))+4(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ (-5\alpha +4\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)+(4\alpha +5\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-5\alpha +4\beta =2\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)) \\ 4\alpha +5\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{10}{41},\beta =\frac{8}{41}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=-\frac{10}{41}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\frac{8}{41}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t)={q}_{c}(t)+{q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-4t}-\frac{10}{41}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\frac{8}{41}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-4t}$ is the *transient charge*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${q}_{p}(t)=-\frac{10}{41}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\frac{8}{41}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)$ is the *steady-state charge*. It governs the charge's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
q(t)≈{q}_{p}(t)=-\frac{10}{41}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\frac{8}{41}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state charge, in coulombs, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{(-\frac{10}{41})}^{2}+{(\frac{8}{41})}^{2}}≈0.31,
$$
